**Mecca**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-4) officially **Makkah al-Mukarramah**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-5) is a city in the [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz") region of western [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") and is the capital of [Mecca Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_Province "Mecca Province").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-6) Mecca is considered the birthplace of [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-8) and the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_and_messengers_in_Islam "Prophets and messengers in Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"), as well as being the [holiest city in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiest_sites_in_Islam "Holiest sites in Islam").

It is located 70 km (43 mi) inland from [Jeddah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeddah "Jeddah") on the [Red Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea "Red Sea") in a narrow valley 277 m (909 ft) above sea level. Its metropolitan population in 2022 was 2.4 million, making it the [third most populated city in Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Saudi_Arabia "List of cities and towns in Saudi Arabia") after [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh") and Jeddah. The [Cave of Hira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal_al-Nour#Cave_of_Hira "Jabal al-Nour") atop the _[Jabal al-Nour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal\_al-Nour "Jabal al-Nour")_ just outside the city is where Muslims believe the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") was first revealed to Muhammad.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-9) The Great Mosque of Mecca, known as the _Masjid al-Haram_, is home to the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba"), believed by Muslims to have been built by [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam") and [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael_in_Islam "Ishmael in Islam"). It is the direction of prayer (_[qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla")_) for all Muslims worldwide.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-10) Around 44.5% of the population are [Saudi citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudis "Saudis") and around 55.5% are [Muslim foreigners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_world "Islamic world") from other countries.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-11) Pilgrims more than triple the population number every year during the _[Ḥajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj")_[pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage#Islam "Pilgrimage"), observed in the twelfth [Hijri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar "Islamic calendar") month of _[Dhūl-Ḥijjah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu\_al-Hijjah "Dhu al-Hijjah")_ as an obligation for all Muslims at least once in their lives.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-12) With over 19.3 million international visitors in 2024, Mecca was one of the five [most visited cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_international_visitors "List of cities by international visitors") in the world.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-13)

Muslim rulers from in and around the region long tried to rule the city, and thus, much like most of the Hejazi region, has seen several [regime changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regime_change "Regime change"). The city was most recently conquered in the [Saudi conquest of Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_conquest_of_Hejaz "Saudi conquest of Hejaz") by [Ibn Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Saud "Ibn Saud") and his allies in [1925](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Mecca_(1924) "Capture of Mecca (1924)"). Since then, Mecca has seen a tremendous expansion in size and infrastructure, with newer, modern buildings such as [The Clock Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clock_Towers "The Clock Towers"), the world's fourth–tallest building and [fifth–largest by floor area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_buildings "List of largest buildings"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-14) towering over the Great Mosque. The [Saudi government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Saudi_Arabia "Politics of Saudi Arabia") has also carried out the [destruction of several historical structures and archaeological sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Britannica-15) such as the [Ajyad Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajyad_Fortress "Ajyad Fortress").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-independent-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-NYT-18) However, many of the demolitions have officially been part of the continued expansion of the Masjid al-Haram at Mecca and the [Prophet's Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque "Prophet's Mosque") in Medina and their auxiliary service facilities in order to accommodate the ever-increasing number of Muslims performing the pilgrimage.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-19) Non-Muslims are [prohibited from entering the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_city "Closed city").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-peters_206-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-21)

Under the Saudi government, Mecca is governed by the Mecca Regional Municipality, a municipal council of 14 locally elected members headed by the mayor (called _Amin_ in Arabic) appointed by the [Saudi government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Saudi_Arabia "Politics of Saudi Arabia"). As of January 2022, the mayor of the city is Saleh Al-Turki.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-22) The City of Mecca _[amanah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdivisions\_of\_Saudi\_Arabia "Subdivisions of Saudi Arabia")_, which constitutes Mecca and the surrounding region, is the capital of the Mecca Province, which includes the neighbouring cities of Jeddah and [Taif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif"), even though Jeddah is considerably larger in population than Mecca. [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud "House of Saud")[Khalid Al-Faisal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Al-Faisal "Khalid Al-Faisal") has been the provincial governor since 16 May 2007.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-23)

## Etymology

Mecca has been referred to by many names. Its [etymology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etymology "Etymology") is obscure as with many Arabic words.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Versteeghp513-24) Widely believed to be a synonym for _Makkah_, it is said to be more specifically the early name for the valley located therein. At the same time, Muslim scholars generally use it to refer to the sacred area of the city that immediately surrounds and includes the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-autogenerated1-25)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Petersonp22-26)

_Makkah_ is the official transliteration used by the Saudi government and is closer to the Arabic pronunciation.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hamp76-27)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-28) The government adopted _Makkah_ as the official spelling in the 1980s, but it is not universally known or used worldwide.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hamp76-27) The full official name is _Makkah al-Mukarramah_ ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مكة المكرمة, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'Makkah the Honored').[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hamp76-27)_Makkah_ is used to refer to the city in the Quran in [Surah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surah "Surah")[Al-Fath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Fath "Al-Fath") (48), verse 24.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Versteeghp513-24)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hittip6-29)

The word _Mecca_ in English has come to be used to refer to any place that draws large numbers of people, and because of this some English-speaking Muslims have come to regard the use of this spelling for the city as offensive.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hamp76-27) Nonetheless, _Mecca_ is the familiar form of the English transliteration for the Arabic name of the city.

_Macoraba_, another ancient city name [Claudius Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy") says was within [Arabia Felix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia_Felix "Arabia Felix"), was also claimed to be Mecca.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-30) Some studies have questioned this association.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Morris-31) Many etymologies have been proposed: the traditional one is that it is derived from the [Old South Arabian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_South_Arabian "Ancient South Arabian") root M-K-R-B which means "temple."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Morris-31)

### Other names

Another name used for Mecca in the Quran is at 6:92 where it is called _Umm al-Qurā_[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-32) (أُمّ ٱلْقُرَى, meaning "Mother of all Settlements").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hittip6-29) The city has been called several other names in both the Quran and _[ahadith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadith "Hadith")_. Another name used historically for Mecca is _[Tihāmah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tihamah "Tihamah")_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-33) According to an Islamic suggestion, another name for Mecca, _Fārān_, is synonymous with the [Desert of Paran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_of_Paran "Desert of Paran") mentioned in the [Hebrew Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_Bible "Hebrew Bible") at [Genesis 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vayeira "Vayeira"):21.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Khanp74-34)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Sefaria-Genesis-21-21-35) Arab and Islamic tradition holds that the wilderness of Paran, broadly speaking, is the [Tihamah coastal plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tihamah "Tihamah") and the site where Ishmael settled was Mecca.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Khanp74-34)[Yaqut al-Hamawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaqut_al-Hamawi "Yaqut al-Hamawi"), the 12th-century Syrian geographer, wrote that _Fārān_ was "an Arabized Hebrew word, one of the names of Mecca mentioned in the Torah."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Firestonep65-36)

#### _Bakkah_

Main article: [Bakkah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakkah "Bakkah")

The Quran refers to the city as [_Bakkah_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakkah "Bakkah") in [Surah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surah "Surah")[Al Imran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Imran "Al Imran") (3), verse 96: "Indeed the first [House [of worship]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_of_worship "Place of worship"), established for mankind was that at Bakkah." This is said to have been the name of the city at the time of [Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam") and it is also transliterated as _Baca, Baka, Bakah, Bakka, Becca_ and _Bekka_, among others.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Kipferp342-37)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Glassep302-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Phippsp85-39) It was a name for the city in the ancient world.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-:2-40)

## History

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Mecca "Timeline of Mecca").

### Prehistory

See also: [Prehistoric Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_Arabia "Prehistoric Arabia")

In 2010, Mecca and the surrounding area became an important site for [paleontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology "Paleontology") with respect to [primate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primate "Primate") evolution, with the discovery of a _[Saadanius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saadanius "Saadanius")_ fossil. _Saadanius_ is considered to be a primate closely related to the common ancestor of the [Old World monkeys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_World_monkey "Old World monkey") and [apes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ape "Ape"). The fossil habitat, near what is now the Red Sea in western Saudi Arabia, was a damp forest area between 28 million and 29 million years ago.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-41) Paleontologists involved in the research hope to find further fossils in the area.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-42)

### Early history (up to 6th century CE)

See also: [Pre-Islamic Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Islamic_Arabia "Pre-Islamic Arabia")

The early history of Mecca is still largely shrouded by a lack of clear sources. The city lies in the hinterland of the middle part of western Arabia of which there are sparse textual or archaeological sources available.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Literary-43) This lack of knowledge is in contrast to both the northern and southern areas of western Arabia, specifically the Syro-Palestinian frontier and Yemen, where historians have various sources available such as physical remains of shrines, inscriptions, observations by Greco-Roman authors, and information collected by church historians. The area of the Hejaz that surrounds Mecca was characterized by its remote, rocky, and inhospitable nature, supporting only meagre settled populations in scattered oases and occasional stretches of fertile land. The Red Sea coast offered no easily accessible ports and the oasis dwellers and bedouins in the region were illiterate.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Literary-43)

One study by Majied Robinson, based on early Islamic genealogical records, estimates that at the time of Muhammad the population of Mecca was around 550.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-44) Muslim scholars using traditional sources may place the number as high as 10,000.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-45)

The first clear reference to Mecca in non-Islamic literature appears in 741, long after the death of Muhammad, in the Byzantine-Arab Chronicle or _[Chronicle of 741](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronicle\_of\_741 "Chronicle of 741")_. However, English writer [Tom Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Holland_(author) "Tom Holland (author)") claims that here the author places the region in [Mesopotamia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesopotamia "Mesopotamia") rather than the Hejaz.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-TH-46)[_[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_]

Possible earlier mentions are ambiguous. The Greek historian [Diodorus Siculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diodorus_Siculus "Diodorus Siculus") writes about Arabia in the 1st century BCE in his work _[Bibliotheca Historica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliotheca\_Historica "Bibliotheca Historica")_, describing a holy shrine: "And a temple has been set up there, which is very holy and exceedingly revered by all Arabians."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-47) Claims have been made this could be a reference to the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-48) However, the geographic location Diodorus describes is located in northwest Arabia, around the area of [Leuke Kome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leuke_Kome "Leuke Kome"), within the former [Nabataean Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabataean_Kingdom "Nabataean Kingdom") and the Roman province of [Arabia Petraea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia_Petraea "Arabia Petraea").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-49)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-50)

Ptolemy lists the names of 50 cities in Arabia, one going by the name of Macoraba. There has been speculation since 1646 that this could be a reference to Mecca. Historically, there has been a general consensus in scholarship that Macoraba mentioned by [Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy") in the 2nd century CE is indeed Mecca, but more recently, this has been questioned.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-52) Historian [Glen Bowersock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Bowersock "Glen Bowersock") favors the identity of the former, with his theory being that "Macoraba" is the word "_Makkah"_ followed by the aggrandizing [Aramaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aramaic "Aramaic") adjective _rabb_ (great). The Roman 4th-century historian [Ammianus Marcellinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammianus_Marcellinus "Ammianus Marcellinus") also enumerated many cities of Western Arabia, most of which can be identified. According to Bowersock, he did mention Mecca as "Geapolis" or "Hierapolis," the latter one meaning "holy city" potentially referring to the sanctuary of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-53) Danish writer [Patricia Crone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Crone "Patricia Crone"), from the [Revisionist school of Islamic studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revisionist_school_of_Islamic_studies "Revisionist school of Islamic studies") on the other hand, writes that "the plain truth is that the name Macoraba has nothing to do with that of Mecca [...] if Ptolemy mentions Mecca at all, he calls it Moka, a town in [Arabia Petraea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia_Petraea "Arabia Petraea")."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-54)

[Procopius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procopius "Procopius")' 6th century statement that the [Ma'add](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma'add "Ma'add") tribe possessed the coast of western Arabia between the [Ghassanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghassanids "Ghassanids") and the [Himyarites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himyar "Himyar") of the south supports the Arabic sources tradition that associates [Quraysh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quraysh "Quraysh") as a branch of the Ma'add and Muhammad as a direct descendant of Ma'add ibn Adnan.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-55)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-56)

Patricia Crone and Tom Holland has cast doubt on the claim that Mecca was a major historical trading outpost.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-ReferenceB-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-58) However, other scholars such as Glen W. Bowersock disagree and assert that Mecca was a major trading outpost.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-59)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-60) Crone later on disregarded some of her theories. She argues that Meccan trade relied on skins, hides, manufactured leather goods, clarified butter, Hijazi woollens, and camels. She suggests that most of these goods were destined for the Roman army, which is known to have required colossal quantities of leather and hides for its equipment.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-61) The earliest Muslim inscriptions are from the Mecca–[Taif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif") area.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-62)

**Islamic narrative**

In the Islamic view, the beginnings of Mecca are attributed to the [Biblical figures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_people_in_Islam "Biblical people in Islam"), [Adam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam "Adam"), [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham "Abraham"), [Hagar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar "Hagar") and [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael "Ishmael"). It was Adam himself who built the first God's house in Mecca according to a heavenly prototype but this building was destroyed in the [Noahic Flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_flood_narrative "Genesis flood narrative").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Literary-43) The civilization of Mecca is believed to have started after [Ibrāhīm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam") (Abraham) left his son Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) and wife [Hājar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam") (Hagar) in the valley at [Allah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allah "Allah")'s command.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Some people from the Yemeni tribe of [Jurhum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurhum "Jurhum") settled with them, and Isma'il reportedly married two women, one after divorcing the first, on Ibrahim's advice. At least one man of the Jurhum helped Ismāʿīl and his father to construct or according to Islamic narratives, reconstruct, the _[Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")_ ('Cube'),[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-63)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-autogenerated1-25)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-64) which would have social, religious, political and historical implications for the site and region.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Glasse1991-65)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Lings1983-66)

Muslims see the mention of a pilgrimage at the [Valley of the Bakha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakkah#Valley_of_the_Bakha "Bakkah") in the [Old Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Testament "Old Testament") chapter [Psalm 84](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_84 "Psalm 84"):3–6 as a reference to Mecca, similar to the Quran at Surah [3:96](https://quran.com/3?startingVerse=96) In the _['āl ʿimrān](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al\_Imran "Al Imran")_, a commentary on the [Samaritan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samaritans "Samaritans")[midrashic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midrash "Midrash") chronology of the Patriarchs, of unknown date but probably composed in the 10th century CE, it is claimed that Mecca was built by the sons of [Nebaioth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebaioth "Nebaioth"), the eldest son of Ismāʿīl or [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael "Ishmael").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-67)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-68)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-69)

#### Under the Quraysh

Sometime in the 5th century, the Ka'bah was a place of worship for the deities of [Arabia's pagan tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_pre-Islamic_Arabia "Religion in pre-Islamic Arabia"). Mecca's most important [pagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paganism "Paganism")[deity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deity "Deity") was [Hubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubal "Hubal"), which had been placed there by the ruling [Quraysh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quraysh "Quraysh") tribe,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-70)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-71) and remained until the [Conquest of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca") by [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In the 5th century, the Quraish took control of Mecca, and became skilled merchants and traders. In the 6th century, they joined the lucrative [spice trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spice_trade "Spice trade"), since battles elsewhere were diverting [trade routes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_route "Trade route") from dangerous sea routes to more secure overland routes. The [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") had previously controlled the [Red Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea "Red Sea"), but [piracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy "Piracy") had been increasing.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Another previous route that ran through the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") via the [Tigris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigris "Tigris") and [Euphrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphrates "Euphrates") rivers was also being threatened by exploitations from the [Sasanian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire"), and was being disrupted by the [Lakhmid kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakhmid_kingdom "Lakhmid kingdom"), the [Ghassanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghassanids "Ghassanids"), and the [Roman–Persian wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman%E2%80%93Persian_wars "Roman–Persian wars"). Mecca's prominence as a trading center also surpassed the cities of [Petra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra "Petra") and [Palmyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra "Palmyra").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-EIE-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-14-73) The Sassanids however did not always pose a threat to Mecca, as in 575 they protected it from a Yemeni invasion, led by its Christian leader [Abraha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraha "Abraha"). The tribes of southern Arabia asked the Persian king [Khosrow I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khosrow_I "Khosrow I") for aid, in response to which he came south to Arabia with foot-soldiers and a fleet of ships near Mecca.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-74)

By the middle of the 6th century, there were three major settlements in northern [Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula"), all along the south-western coast that borders the Red Sea, in a habitable region between the sea and the Hejaz mountains to the east. Although the area around Mecca was completely barren, it was the wealthiest of the three settlements with abundant water from the renowned [Zamzam Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well") and a position at the crossroads of major [caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camel_train "Camel train") routes.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-world-13-75)

The harsh conditions and terrain of the Arabian peninsula meant a near-constant state of conflict between the [local tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribes_of_Arabia "Tribes of Arabia"), but once a year they would declare a truce and converge upon Mecca in an annual pilgrimage. Up to the 7th century, this journey was intended for religious reasons by the pagan Arabs to pay homage to their shrine, and to drink [Zamzam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"). However, it was also the time each year that disputes would be arbitrated, debts would be resolved, and trading would occur at Meccan fairs. These annual events gave the tribes a sense of common identity and made Mecca an important focus for the peninsula.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-16-76)

#### Year of the Elephant (570)

The "[Year of the Elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Elephant "Year of the Elephant")" is the name in [Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") history for the year approximately equating to 570–572, when, according to Islamic sources such as [Ibn Ishaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Ishaq "Ibn Ishaq"), [Abraha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraha "Abraha") descended upon Mecca, riding an elephant, with a large army after building a [cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_(building) "Church (building)") at [San'aa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanaa "Sanaa"), named _al-Qullays_ in honor of the [Negus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negus "Negus") of [Axum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axum "Axum"). It gained widespread fame, even gaining attention from the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"). Abraha attempted to divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs from the Ka'bah to al-Qullays, effectively converting them to Christianity. According to Islamic tradition, this was the year of Muhammad's birth. Abraha allegedly sent a messenger named Muhammad ibn Khuza'i to Mecca and [Tihamah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tihamah "Tihamah") with a message that al-Qullays was both much better than other houses of worship and purer, having not been defiled by the housing of idols.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hajjah-77) When Muhammad ibn Khuza'i got as far as the land of [Banu Kinana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinana "Kinana"), the people of the lowland, knowing what he had come for, sent a man of [Hudhayl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Hudhayl "Banu Hudhayl") called ʿUrwa bin Hayyad al-Milasi, who shot him with an arrow, killing him. His brother Qays who was with him, fled to Abraha and told him the news, which increased his rage and fury and he swore to raid the Kinana tribe and destroy the Ka'bah. Ibn Ishaq further states that one of the men of the [Quraysh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quraysh "Quraysh") tribe was angered by this, and going to Sana'a, entering the church at night and defiling it; widely assumed to have done so by [defecating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defecation "Defecation") in it.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-DACB-78)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Muller-79)

Abraha marched upon the Kaaba with a large army, which included one or more [war elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_elephant "War elephant"), intending to demolish it. When news of the advance of his army came, the Arab tribes of Quraysh, Kinanah, [Banu Khuza'ah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Khuza'ah "Banu Khuza'ah") and Hudhayl united in the defense of the Kaaba and the city. A man from the [Himyarite Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himyar "Himyar") was sent by Abraha to advise them that Abraha only wished to demolish the Ka'bah and if they resisted, they would be crushed. [Abd al-Muttalib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Muttalib "Abd al-Muttalib") told the Meccans to seek refuge in the hills while he and some members of the Quraysh remained within the precincts of the Kaaba. Abraha sent a dispatch inviting Abdul-Muttalib to meet with Abraha and discuss matters. When Abdul-Muttalib left the meeting he was heard saying: "The Owner of this House is its Defender, and I am sure he will save it from the attack of the adversaries and will not dishonor the servants of His House."[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-80)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-81)

Abraha eventually attacked Mecca. However, the lead elephant, known as Mahmud,[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-82) is said to have stopped at the boundary around Mecca and refused to enter. It has been theorized that an epidemic such as by [smallpox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox "Smallpox") could have caused such a failed invasion of Mecca.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-83) The reference to the story in [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") is rather short. According to the 105th [Surah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surah "Surah") of the Quran, [Al-Fil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Fil "Al-Fil"), the next day, a dark cloud of small birds sent by Allah appeared. The birds carried small rocks in their beaks, and bombarded the Ethiopian forces, and smashed them to a state like that of eaten straw.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-84)

#### Economy

See also: [Economy and trade of pre-Islamic Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_and_trade_of_pre-Islamic_Arabia "Economy and trade of pre-Islamic Arabia")

Camel caravans, said to have first been used by Muhammad's great-grandfather, were a major part of Mecca's bustling economy. Alliances were struck between the merchants in Mecca and the local nomadic tribes, who would bring goods – leather, livestock, and metals mined in the local mountains – to Mecca to be loaded on the caravans and carried to cities in [Shaam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria_(region) "Syria (region)") and [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-world-85) Historical accounts also provide some indication that goods from other continents may also have flowed through Mecca. Goods from Africa and the Far East passed through en route to Syria including spices, leather, medicine, cloth, and slaves; in return Mecca received money, weapons, cereals, and wine, which in turn were distributed throughout Arabia.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The Meccans signed treaties with both the Byzantines and the [Bedouins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedouin "Bedouin"), and negotiated safe passages for caravans, giving them water and pasture rights. Mecca became the center of a loose confederation of client tribes, which included those of the [Banu Tamim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Tamim "Banu Tamim"). Other regional powers such as the [Abyssinians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habesha_peoples "Habesha peoples"), Ghassanids, and Lakhmids were in decline leaving Meccan trade to be the primary binding force in Arabia in the late 6th century.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-16-76)

### Muhammad and the conquest of Mecca

Main articles: [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"), [Conquest of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca"), [Muhammad in Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Mecca "Muhammad in Mecca"), and [List of expeditions of Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_expeditions_of_Muhammad "List of expeditions of Muhammad")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Site_of_the_birthplace_of_the_Prophet_Muhammad%2C_Mecca%2C_Saudi_Arabia.jpg/250px-Site_of_the_birthplace_of_the_Prophet_Muhammad%2C_Mecca%2C_Saudi_Arabia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Site_of_the_birthplace_of_the_Prophet_Muhammad,_Mecca,_Saudi_Arabia.jpg)

[Makkah Al Mukarramah Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makkah_Al_Mukarramah_Library "Makkah Al Mukarramah Library") is believed to stand on the spot where Muhammad was born, so it is also known as the _Bayt al-Mawlid_ (House of the Birth)

Muhammad was [born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mawlid "Mawlid") in Mecca in 570, and thus Islam has been inextricably linked with it ever since. He was born into the faction of [Banu Hashim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Hashim "Banu Hashim") in the ruling tribe of [Quraysh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quraysh "Quraysh"). It was in the nearby mountain cave of Hira on [Jabal al-Nour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal_al-Nour "Jabal al-Nour") that Muhammad began receiving divine [revelations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revelation "Revelation") from God through the [archangel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archangel "Archangel")[Jibreel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel "Gabriel") in 610, according to Islamic tradition. Advocating his form of [Abrahamic monotheism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abrahamic_religions "Abrahamic religions") against Meccan paganism, and after enduring persecution from the pagan tribes for 13 years, Muhammad emigrated ([Hijrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah "Hijrah")) in 622 with his companions, the _[Muhajirun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhajirun "Muhajirun")_, to Yathrib (later renamed [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina")). The conflict between the Quraysh and the Muslims is accepted to have begun at this point. Overall, Meccan efforts to annihilate Islam failed and proved to be costly and unsuccessful.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-86) During the [Battle of the Trench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Trench "Battle of the Trench") in 627, the combined armies of Arabia were unable to defeat Muhammad's forces (as the trench surrounding Muhammad's forces protected them from harm and a storm was sent to breach the Quraysh tribe).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-32-87) In 628, Muhammad and his followers wanted to enter Mecca for pilgrimage, but were blocked by the Quraysh. Subsequently, Muslims and Meccans entered into the [Treaty of al-Hudaybiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_al-Hudaybiya "Treaty of al-Hudaybiya"), whereby the Quraysh and their allies promised to cease fighting Muslims and their allies and pledged to permit Muslims into the city to perform the pilgrimage the following year. It was meant to be a ceasefire for 10 years; however, just two years later, the [Banu Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Bakr "Banu Bakr"), allies of the Quraish, violated the truce by slaughtering a group of the Banu Khuza'ah, allies of the Muslims. Muhammad and his companions, now 10,000 strong, marched into Mecca and conquered the city. The pagan imagery was destroyed by Muhammad's followers and the location [Islamized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spread_of_Islam "Spread of Islam") and rededicated to the worship of [Allah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allah "Allah") alone. Mecca was declared the holiest site in Islam ordaining it as the center of Muslim pilgrimage (_[Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj")_), one of the Islamic faith's [Five Pillars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Pillars_of_Islam "Five Pillars of Islam").

Muhammad then returned to Medina, after assigning [Attab ibn Asid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attab_ibn_Asid "Attab ibn Asid") as governor of the city. His other activities in Arabia led to the unification of the Arabian Peninsula under the banner of Islam.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-EIE-72)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-32-87) Muhammad died in 632. Within the next few hundred years, the area under the banner of Islam stretched from North Africa into Asia and parts of Europe. As the [Islamic realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate "Rashidun Caliphate") grew, Mecca continued to attract pilgrims from all across the [Muslim world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_world "Islamic world") and beyond, as Muslims came to perform the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Mecca attracted a year-round population of scholars, pious Muslims who wished to live close to the Kaaba, and local inhabitants who served the pilgrims. Due to the difficulty and expense of the Hajj, pilgrims arrived by boat at Jeddah, and came overland, or joined the annual caravans from Syria or Iraq.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-88)

### Medieval and pre-modern times

Mecca was never the capital of any of the [Islamic states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate "Caliphate") except the [Zubayrid Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr"). Muslim rulers did contribute to its upkeep, such as during the reigns of '[Umar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar "Umar") (r. 634–644) and [Uthman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthman "Uthman") (r. 644–656) when concerns of flooding caused the caliphs to bring in Christian engineers to build barrages in the low-lying quarters and construct dykes and embankments to protect the area around the Kaaba.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-EIE-72)

Muhammad's return to Medina shifted the focus away from Mecca and later even further away when '[Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali "Ali"), the fourth caliph, took power and chose [Kufa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kufa "Kufa") as his capital. The [Umayyad Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate "Umayyad Caliphate") moved the capital to [Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus "Damascus") in Syria and the [Abbasid Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") to [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad"), in modern-day Iraq, which remained the center of the Islamic Empire for nearly 500 years. Mecca re-entered Islamic political history during the [Second Fitna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Fitna "Second Fitna"), when it was held by [Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr") and the Zubayrids.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The city was twice besieged by the Umayyads in [683](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mecca_(683) "Siege of Mecca (683)") and [692](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mecca_(692) "Siege of Mecca (692)"), and for some time thereafter, the city figured little in politics, remaining a city of devotion and scholarship governed by various other factions. In 930, Mecca was [attacked and sacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Mecca "Sack of Mecca") by [Qarmatians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qarmatians "Qarmatians"), a [millenarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millenarianism "Millenarianism")[Shi'a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shia_Islam "Shia Islam")[Isma'ili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismailism "Ismailism")[Muslim sect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_schools_and_branches "Islamic schools and branches") led by [Abu Tahir al-Jannabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Tahir_al-Jannabi "Abu Tahir al-Jannabi") and centered in eastern Arabia.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-89) The [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death")[pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemic "Pandemic") hit Mecca in 1349.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-90)

#### Ibn Battuta's description of Mecca

One of the most famous travelers to Mecca in the 14th century was a Moroccan scholar and traveler, [Ibn Battuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Battuta "Ibn Battuta"). In his _rihla_ (account), he provides a vast description of the city. Around the year 1327 (729 AH), Ibn Battuta arrived at the holy city. Immediately, he says, it felt like a holy sanctuary, and thus he started the rites of the pilgrimage. He remained in Mecca for three years and left in 1330. During his second year in the holy city, he says his caravan arrived "with a great quantity of alms for the support of those who were staying in Mecca and Medina." While in Mecca, prayers were made for (not to) the King of Iraq and also for [Salaheddin al-Ayyubi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saladin "Saladin"), Sultan of Egypt and Syria at the Ka'bah. Battuta says the Ka'bah was large, but was destroyed and rebuilt smaller than the original. According to Ibn Battuta, the original Kaaba, prior to the conquest of Makkah by the Prophet, contained images of angels and prophets including Jesus (Isa in Islamic tradition), his mother Mary (Maryam in Islamic tradition), and many others - Ibn Battuta however states these were all destroyed by the Prophet in the year of victory. Battuta describes the Ka'bah in his time as an important part of Mecca due to the fact that many people make the pilgrimage to it. Battuta describes the people of the city as being humble and kind, and also willing to give a part of everything they had to someone who had nothing. The inhabitants of Mecca and the village itself, he says, were very clean. There was also a sense of elegance to the village.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-91)

#### Under the Ottomans

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Khalili_Collection_Hajj_Mecca_panorama.jpg/250px-Khalili_Collection_Hajj_Mecca_panorama.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Khalili_Collection_Hajj_Mecca_panorama.jpg)

Panorama of Mecca, 1845, from the [Khalili Collection of Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalili_Collection_of_Hajj_and_the_Arts_of_Pilgrimage "Khalili Collection of Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage")

In 1517, the Sharif of Mecca, Barakat bin Muhammad, acknowledged the supremacy of the [Ottoman Caliph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Caliphate "Ottoman Caliphate") but retained a great degree of local autonomy.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-92) In 1803 the city was captured by the [First Saudi state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Saudi_state "First Saudi state"),[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-93) which held Mecca until 1813, destroying some of the historic tombs and domes in and around the city. The Ottomans assigned the task of bringing Mecca back under Ottoman control to their powerful _[Khedive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khedive "Khedive")_ (viceroy) and _[Wali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wali\_(administrative\_title) "Wali (administrative title)")_ of Egypt, [Muhammad Ali Pasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_of_Egypt "Muhammad Ali of Egypt"). Muhammad Ali Pasha successfully returned Mecca to Ottoman control [in 1813](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Mecca_(1813) "Capture of Mecca (1813)"). In 1818, the Saud were defeated again but survived and founded the [Second Saudi state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Saudi_state "Second Saudi state") that lasted until 1891 and led on to the present country of Saudi Arabia. In 1853, Sir [Richard Francis Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Francis_Burton "Richard Francis Burton") undertook the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina disguised as a Muslim. Although Burton was certainly not the first non-Muslim European to make the _Hajj_ ([Ludovico di Varthema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovico_di_Varthema "Ludovico di Varthema") did this in 1503),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-94)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Webb_01-2023-95) his pilgrimage remains one of the most famous and documented of modern times. Mecca was regularly hit by [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera")[outbreaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_cholera "History of cholera"). Between 1830 and 1930, cholera broke out among pilgrims at Mecca 27 times.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-96)

### Modern history

Mecca in 1910

#### Hashemite revolt and subsequent control by the Sharifate of Mecca

In [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the Ottoman Empire was at war with the [Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_I "Allies of World War I"). It had successfully repulsed an attack on [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") in the [Gallipoli campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallipoli_campaign "Gallipoli campaign") and on Baghdad in the [Siege of Kut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Kut "Siege of Kut"). The British intelligence officer [T. E. Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._E._Lawrence "T. E. Lawrence") conspired with the Ottoman governor, [Hussain bin Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussein,_King_of_Hejaz "Hussein, King of Hejaz"), the Sharif of Mecca to revolt against the Ottoman Empire and it was the first city captured by his forces in the [Battle of Mecca (1916)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mecca_(1916) "Battle of Mecca (1916)"). Sharif's revolt proved a turning point of the war on the eastern front. Hussein declared a new state, the [Kingdom of Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hejaz "Kingdom of Hejaz"), declaring himself the Sharif of the state and Mecca his capital. News reports in November 1916 via contact in [Cairo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo "Cairo") with returning Hajj pilgrims, stated that with the Ottoman Turkish authorities gone, the Hajj of 1916 was free of the previous massive extortion and monetary demands made by the Turks who were agents of the Ottoman government.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-97)

#### Saudi conquest

Following the [Capture of Mecca (1924)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Mecca_(1924) "Capture of Mecca (1924)"), the Sharif of Mecca was overthrown by the Saud family, and Mecca was incorporated into Saudi Arabia.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-encarta-98) Under Saudi rule, much of the historic city has been demolished as a result of the Saudi government fearing these sites might become sites of association in worship besides Allah (_[shirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirk\_(Islam) "Shirk (Islam)")_). The city has been expanded to include several towns previously considered to be separate from the holy city and now is just a few kilometers outside the main sites of the Hajj, Mina, Muzdalifah, and Arafat. Mecca is not served by any airport, due to concerns about the city's safety. It is instead served by the [King Abdulaziz International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_International_Airport "King Abdulaziz International Airport") in [Jeddah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeddah "Jeddah") (approx. 70 km away) internationally and the [Taif International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif_International_Airport "Taif International Airport") (approx. 120 km away) for domestic flights.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The city today is at the junction of the two most important highways in all of the Saudi Arabian highway system, Highway 40, which connects the city to Jeddah in the west and the capital, [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh") and [Dammam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dammam "Dammam") in the east and Highway 15, which connects it to [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), [Tabuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabuk,_Saudi_Arabia "Tabuk, Saudi Arabia") and onward to [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan") in the north and [Abha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abha "Abha") and [Jizan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jizan "Jizan") in the south. The Ottomans had planned to extend their railway network to the holy city, but were forced to abandon this plan due to their entry into [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). This plan was later carried out by the Saudi government, which connected the two holy cities of Medina and Mecca with the modern [Haramain High Speed Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haramain_High_Speed_Railway "Haramain High Speed Railway") system which runs at 300 km/h (190 mph) and connects the two cities via Jeddah, King Abdulaziz International Airport and [King Abdullah Economic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdullah_Economic_City "King Abdullah Economic City") near Rabigh within two hours.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The [haram area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haram_(site) "Haram (site)") of Mecca, in which the entry of non-Muslims is forbidden, is much larger than that of Medina.

#### 1979 Grand Mosque seizure

See also: [Grand Mosque seizure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure "Grand Mosque seizure")

On 20 November 1979, two hundred armed dissidents led by [Juhayman al-Otaybi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juhayman_al-Otaybi "Juhayman al-Otaybi"), [seized the Grand Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure "Grand Mosque seizure"), claiming the Saudi royal family no longer represented pure Islam and that the Masjid al-Haram and the Ka'bah, must be held by those of true faith. The rebels seized tens of thousands of pilgrims as hostages and barricaded themselves in the mosque. The siege lasted two weeks, and resulted in several hundred deaths and significant damage to the shrine, especially the [Safa and Marwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safa_and_Marwa "Safa and Marwa") gallery. A multinational force was finally able to retake the mosque from the dissidents.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-99) Since then, the Grand Mosque has been expanded several times, with many other expansions being undertaken in the present day.

#### Destruction of Islamic heritage sites

Main article: [Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Makkah_Aerial_View.jpg/330px-Makkah_Aerial_View.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makkah_Aerial_View.jpg)

Mecca, as seen from [Jabal al-Nour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal_al-Nour "Jabal al-Nour"). [The Clock Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clock_Towers "The Clock Towers") is visible in the skyline.

Under Saudi rule, it has been estimated that since 1985, about 95% of Mecca's historic buildings, most over a thousand years old, have been demolished.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-independent-16)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-independent.co.uk-100) It has been reported that there are now fewer than 20 structures remaining in Mecca that date back to the time of Muhammad. Some important buildings that have been destroyed include the house of [Khadijah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khadija_bint_Khuwaylid "Khadija bint Khuwaylid"), the wife of Muhammad, the house of [Abu Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Bakr "Abu Bakr"), Muhammad's birthplace, and the Ottoman–era [Ajyad Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajyad_Fortress "Ajyad Fortress").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-101) The reason for much of the destruction of historic buildings has been for the construction of hotels, apartments, parking lots, and other infrastructure facilities for Hajj pilgrims.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-independent.co.uk-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-102)

#### Incidents during pilgrimage

Main article: [Incidents during the Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidents_during_the_Hajj "Incidents during the Hajj")

Mecca has been the site of several incidents and failures of crowd control because of the large numbers of people who come to make the Hajj.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-103)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-104)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-105) For example, on 2 July 1990, a pilgrimage to Mecca ended in tragedy when the ventilation system failed in a crowded pedestrian tunnel and 1,426 people were either suffocated or trampled to death in a [stampede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Mecca_tunnel_tragedy "1990 Mecca tunnel tragedy").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-106) On 24 September 2015, 700 pilgrims [were killed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Mina_stampede "2015 Mina stampede") in a stampede at [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina,_Saudi_Arabia "Mina, Saudi Arabia") during the stoning-the-Devil ritual at Jamarat.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-107)

#### 2027 total solar eclipse

Mecca will experience a [total solar eclipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_eclipse_of_August_2,_2027 "Solar eclipse of August 2, 2027") on Monday, 2 August 2027, for a duration of 5 minutes and 8 seconds.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-108)

## Significance in Islam

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/La_Mecque_pelerinage.png/330px-La_Mecque_pelerinage.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:La_mecque_pelerinage.png)

The [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") involves pilgrims visiting Al-Haram Mosque, but mainly camping and spending time in the plains of [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina,_Saudi_Arabia "Mina, Saudi Arabia") and [Arafah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arafah "Arafah")

Mecca holds an important place in Islam and is considered the holiest city in all branches of the religion. The city derives its importance from the role it plays in the [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and '[Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah") and for its status as the birthplace of Muhammad.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Webb_01-2023-95)

### Masjid al-Haram

The _Masjid al-Haram_ is the site of two of the most important rites of both the Hajj and of the Umrah, the circumambulation around the Ka'bah (_[tawaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawaf "Tawaf")_) and the walking between the two mounts of Safa and Marwa (_[sa'ee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sa'ee "Sa'ee")_). The masjid is also the site of the [Zamzam Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"). According to Islamic tradition, a prayer in the masjid is equal to 100,000 prayers in any other masjid around the world.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-109)

**Masjid al-Haram** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): المسجد الحرام, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-Masjid al-Ḥarām_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'The Sacred Mosque'),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-4) also known as the **Great Mosque of Mecca**,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-5) is a [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") in Mecca, [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), serving as the holiest and most important mosque in [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-7)As of 2026,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit) the Great Mosque is the [largest mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_mosques "List of largest mosques") in the world.

The Great Mosque is considered, alongside the [Quba Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quba_Mosque "Quba Mosque") in [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), among the earliest mosques in Islam.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-8) According to Islamic scholars, Abraham is seen as having built the _Kaaba_ in Mecca, and consequently its sanctuary, which according to the Muslim view is seen as the first mosque[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-Palmer20163-9) that ever existed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-12)

It has undergone major renovations and expansions through the years.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-13) It has passed through the control of various [caliphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphs "Caliphs"), [sultans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sultans_of_the_Ottoman_Empire "List of sultans of the Ottoman Empire") and kings, and is now under the control of the [King of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Saudi_Arabia "King of Saudi Arabia") who is titled the [Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custodian_of_the_Two_Holy_Mosques "Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-14)

It encloses the vicinity of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca, in the [western region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz") of the country. It is among the pilgrimage sites associated with the [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj"), which every [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") according to orthodox Islamic belief, must perform at least once in their lives if able. It is also the main site for the performance of ʿ[Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah"), the lesser pilgrimage that can be undertaken any time of the year. The rites of both pilgrimages include [circumambulating the Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawaf "Tawaf") within the mosque. The Great Mosque contains other important sites, such as the [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone"), the [Zamzam Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"), [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim"), and the hills of [Safa and Marwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safa_and_Marwa "Safa and Marwa").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-15)

Further information: [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), [History of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Islam "History of Islam"), [History of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia "History of Saudi Arabia"), and [Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_architecture "Islamic architecture")

In the [pre-Islamic religions of Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_pre-Islamic_Arabia "Religion in pre-Islamic Arabia") -spanning from the [Levant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levant "Levant") to [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"), [numerous deities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_pre-Islamic_Arabian_deities "List of pre-Islamic Arabian deities") —such as, [Al-Lat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Lat "Al-Lat"), [Dhu al-Khalasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Khalasa "Dhu al-Khalasa"), and [al-Uzza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Uzza "Al-Uzza") (also occasionally referred to as [Chaabou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaabou "Chaabou")), [Dushara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dushara "Dushara"), [Dhu Samawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_Samawi "Dhu Samawi") etc.— were represented by [aniconic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aniconism "Aniconism") cubic stone carvings or by cubic structures regarded as [the abodes of these deities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaabas "Kaabas"); furthermore, the existence of "sacred/haram zones" surrounding these sanctuaries and the widespread use of [the name "Ka'b"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ka'b "Ka'b") to denote such sanctity, is well-established.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-16) Although the cultural heritage of the pagan era was largely eradicated during Islam's struggle to establish [Islamic monotheism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawhid "Tawhid"), historical research has uncovered traces of some [sanctuaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctuary "Sanctuary") that were significant enough to rival the Kaaba in Mecca; nevertheless, the belief that there has always been only one Kaaba has become deeply ingrained in Muslim literary and religious tradition. Today, the Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca are identified as the direction of prayer; however, an archaeological document found in the [Taif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif") region suggests that this view is anachronistic from the perspective of traditional Islamic historiography, as a stone inscription discovered there dates the construction of the Masjid al-Haram to the year 78 AH.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-17) Furthermore, a Quranic verse recounting [Muhammad's night journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra'_and_Mi'raj "Isra' and Mi'raj") —an event often presented today as a miracle— to the [Masjid al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Aqsa "Masjid al-Aqsa") offers clues suggesting that the *Masjid al-Haram* mentioned in the Quran might differ from the one located in Mecca. [Surah Al-Isra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Isra "Al-Isra")[17:1](https://quran.com/17?startingVerse=1):

> Glory be to the One Who took His servant by night from Masjid al-Haram to the [Masjid al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa_Mosque "Al-Aqsa Mosque") whose surroundings We have blessed, so that We may show him some of Our signs. Indeed, He alone is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing

The significance of mosque structures from the early Islamic period that face in different directions continues to be a subject of serious debate between [revisionist historians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revisionist_school_of_Islamic_studies "Revisionist school of Islamic studies") and conservatives.

### Era of Abraham and Ishmael

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Era of Abraham and Ishmael")]

See also: [Abraham in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam"), [Hagar in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam"), and [Ishmael in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael_in_Islam "Ishmael in Islam")

According to Islamic tradition in the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran"), [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam"), together with his son [Ismael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael_in_Islam "Ishmael in Islam"), raised the foundations of a house,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-18) which has been identified by commentators as the Kaaba. According to Islamic tradition, it is said that Allah showed Abraham the exact site, which was previously built by [Adam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_in_Islam "Adam in Islam"), very near to what is now the [Well of Zamzam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well_of_Zamzam "Well of Zamzam"). After Abraham had built the Kaaba, an angel is said to have brought him the [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone"), a celestial stone that, according to tradition, had fallen from Heaven on the nearby hill [Abu Qubays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Qubays_(mountain) "Abu Qubays (mountain)"). The Black Stone is believed by Islamic scholars to be the only remnant of the original structure made by Abraham.

After placing the Black Stone in the Eastern corner of the Kaaba, Abraham reportedly received a revelation in which God told the aged prophet that he should now go and proclaim the pilgrimage to mankind, so that men may come both from Arabia and from lands far away, on camel and on foot.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-19)

### Era of Muhammad

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Era of Muhammad")]

Main article: [Muhammad in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam")

Upon Muhammad's [victorious return to Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca") in 630 [CE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era"), he and a number of the _[Sahaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahaba "Sahaba")_ including Ali broke the idols in and around the Kaaba,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-20) similar to what, according to the Quran, Abraham did in his homeland. This ended polytheistic use of the Kaaba, and began monotheistic rule over it and its sanctuary.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-24)

### Rashidun era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rashidun era")]

The mosque has been expanded by [caliph Umar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar "Umar") in 637 CE by 1,500 m 2, in response to the increasing number of Muslims, its area has reached a total of 3,600 m 2, another expansion was carried out by [caliph Uthman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthman "Uthman") where the covered porticoes have been introduced for the first time.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:7-25)

### Umayyad era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Umayyad era")]

In 682, the ruler of Mecca [Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr"), who opposed the Umayyads following the death of [Mu'awiya I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu'awiya_I "Mu'awiya I") carried an expansion that increased the total area to 7,465 m 2,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:7-25) and following [the reconquest of Mecca by the Umayyads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mecca_(692) "Siege of Mecca (692)") in 692, the first major renovation to the mosque took place on the orders of [Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Malik_ibn_Marwan "Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-26) Before this renovation, which included the mosque's outer walls being raised, the mosque was a small open area with the Kaaba at the center. By the end of the 8th century, the mosque's old wooden columns had been replaced with marble columns and the wings of the prayer hall had been extended on both sides along with the addition of a [minaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret") on the orders of [Al-Walid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Walid_I "Al-Walid I").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-28)

### Abbasid era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Abbasid era")]

The next expansion of the mosque was sponsored by the [Abbasid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") caliph [al-Mansur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mansur "Al-Mansur") between 754 and 757.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:16-29) This was followed by a major expansion begun by his successor, Caliph [al-Mahdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mahdi "Al-Mahdi"), in 779. This work was completed shortly after him by his successor, Caliph [al-Hadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Hadi "Al-Hadi") (r.785–786),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:6-30) which made the made the mosque's total area to reach 28,000 m 2, this was the largest expansion to the size of the mosque until the Saudi era,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:7-25) except for two further extensions by the caliph [al-Mu'tadid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mu'tadid "Al-Mu'tadid") in 894–5 and by the caliph [al-Muqtadir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Muqtadir "Al-Muqtadir") in 918,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:6-30) but it retained its overall form from this period until the later [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") renovations.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:16-29)

### Ottoman era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Ottoman era")]

In 1570, [Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Sultan "Ottoman Sultan")[Selim II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selim_II "Selim II") commissioned the chief architect [Mimar Sinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimar_Sinan "Mimar Sinan") to renovate the mosque. This renovation resulted in the replacement of the flat roof with domes decorated with [calligraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calligraphy "Islamic calligraphy") internally, and the placement of new support columns which are acknowledged as the earliest architectural features of the present mosque. These features are the oldest surviving parts of the building.

During heavy rains and flash floods in 1621 and 1629, the walls of the Kaaba and the mosque suffered extensive damage.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-31) In 1629, during the reign of Sultan [Murad IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_IV "Murad IV"), the mosque was renovated. In the renovation of the mosque, a new stone arcade was added, three more minarets (bringing the total to seven) were built, and the marble flooring was retiled. This was the unaltered state of the mosque for nearly three centuries, the Ottoman era renovations did not expand the size of the mosque.
