### The Saudi era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The Saudi era")]

#### First Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: First Saudi expansion")]

The first major renovation under the Saudi kings was done between 1955 and 1976. In this renovation, four more minarets were added, the ceiling was refurnished, and the floor was replaced with artificial stone and marble. The Mas'a gallery (As-Safa and Al-Marwah) is included in the Mosque, via roofing and enclosures. During this renovation many of the historical features built by the Ottomans, particularly the support columns, were [demolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia").

On 20 November 1979, the Great Mosque was [seized by extremist insurgents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure "Grand Mosque seizure") who called for the overthrow of the Saudi dynasty. They took hostages and in the ensuing siege hundreds were killed. These events came as a shock to the Islamic world, as violence is strictly forbidden within the mosque.

#### Second Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Second Saudi expansion")]

The second Saudi renovations under [King Fahd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Fahd "King Fahd"), added a new wing and an outdoor prayer area to the mosque. The new wing, which is also for prayers, is reached through the King Fahd Gate. This extension was performed between 1986 and 1994.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-32)

1987 to 2005 saw the building of more minarets, the erecting of a [King's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Saudi_Arabia "King of Saudi Arabia") residence overlooking the mosque and more prayer area in and around the mosque itself. These developments took place simultaneously with those in [Arafat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Arafat "Mount Arafat"), [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina,_Saudi_Arabia "Mina, Saudi Arabia") and [Muzdalifah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muzdalifah "Muzdalifah"). This extension also added 18 more gates, three domes corresponding in position to each gate and the installation of nearly 500 marble columns. Other modern developments added heated floors, air conditioning, escalators and a drainage system.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In addition, the King Fahd expansion includes 6 dedicated prayer halls for people with disabilities. These halls have ramps to facilitate entry and exit with wheelchairs, as well as dedicated paths and free electric and manual carts for their use.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-33)

#### Third Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Third Saudi expansion")]

In 2008, the Saudi government under [King Abdullah Ibn Abdulaziz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia "Abdullah of Saudi Arabia") announced an expansion[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-34) of the mosque, involving the [expropriation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expropriation "Expropriation") of land to the north and northwest of the mosque covering 300,000 m 2 (3,200,000 sq ft). At that time, the mosque covered an area of 356,800 m 2 (3,841,000 sq ft) including indoor and outdoor praying spaces. 40 billion riyals (US$10.6 billion) was allocated for the expansion project.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-35) In August 2011, the government under [King Abdullah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia "Abdullah of Saudi Arabia") announced further details of the expansion. It would cover an area of 400,000 m 2 (4,300,000 ft 2) and accommodate 1.2 million worshippers, including a multi-level extension on the north side of the complex, new stairways and tunnels, a gate named after King Abdullah, and two minarets, bringing the total number of minarets to eleven. The circumambulation areas (Mataf) around the Kaaba would be expanded and all closed spaces receive air conditioning. After completion, it would raise the mosque's capacity from 770,000 to over 2.5 million worshippers.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:3-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:5-37)[His successor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_kings_of_Saudi_Arabia "List of kings of Saudi Arabia"), [King Salman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia "Salman of Saudi Arabia") launched five megaprojects as part of the overall King Abdullah Expansion Project in July 2015, covering an area of 456,000 m 2 (4,910,000 sq ft). The project was carried out by the [Saudi Binladin Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Binladin_Group "Saudi Binladin Group").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-38) In 2012, the [Abraj Al Bait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraj_Al_Bait "Abraj Al Bait") complex was completed along with the 601-meter-tall (1,972 ft) Makkah Royal Clock Tower. Austrian company Lights of Vienna was hired to complete a 100 million euro order of 4700 chandeliers and light fixtures in 26 sizes in 2013. The chandeliers and light fixtures were installed in the Shamiya Extension of the mosque. Some of the biggest gilded chandeliers were priced at 1 million euros each. The company has since been the provider of additional light fixtures to the mosque and other buildings in Mecca.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-39) In 2025, the lighting for the Mataf extension was completed by Lights of Vienna. The project involved the delivery of 10 different lighting types and a total of around 550 custom-made chandeliers and luminaires, all produced from high-grade stainless steel and gilded with more than 200 kg of 24-karat gold. The project value is approximately €90 million. Part of the new lights was the 7-metre _Al Fath Gate Chandelier_, an octagonal, gold-plated chandelier with a 7-meter diameter and 360,000 lumens of output. All fixtures incorporate high-efficiency LED systems.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-41)

On 11 September 2015, at least 111 people died and 394 were injured [when a crane collapsed onto the mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_crane_collapse "Mecca crane collapse").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-46) Construction work was suspended after the incident, and remained on hold due to financial issues during the [2010s oil glut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010s_oil_glut "2010s oil glut"). Development was eventually restarted two years later in September 2017.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-47)

#### COVID-19 Pandemic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: COVID-19 Pandemic")]

On 5 March 2020, during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the mosque began to be closed at night and the Umrah pilgrimage was suspended to limit attendance.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-48) The resumption of Umrah service began on 4 October 2020 with the first phase of a gradual resumption that was limited to Saudi citizens and expatriates from within the Kingdom at a rate of 30 percent.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-49) Only 10,000 people were given Hajj visas in 2020 while 60,000 people were given visas in 2021.

## Pilgrimage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Pilgrimage")]

Main articles: [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah")

The Great Mosque is the main setting for the Hajj and Umrah pilgrimages[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-50) that occur in the month of [Dhu al-Hijja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Hijja "Dhu al-Hijja") in the [Islamic calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar "Islamic calendar") and at any time of the year, respectively. The Hajj pilgrimage is one of the Pillars of Islam, required of all able-bodied Muslims who can afford the trip. In recent times, over 5 million Muslims perform the Hajj every year.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-51)

## Notable structures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Notable structures")]

### Kaaba

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Kaaba")]

Main article: [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah%2C_Saudi_Arabia_%2852501405646%29.jpg/250px-The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah%2C_Saudi_Arabia_%2852501405646%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah,_Saudi_Arabia_(52501405646).jpg)

The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")

The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") is a [cuboid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuboid "Cuboid")-shaped building in the centre of the Masjid al-Haram and is the [most sacred site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_significant_religious_sites#Islam "List of significant religious sites") in Islam.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-eoi317-52) It is the [qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla")_(direction of prayer)_ for [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") worldwide. It is the focal point of the [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah") rites. The [pilgrims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage "Pilgrimage") perform the _tawaf_ (circumambulation) around its exterior.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-eoi317-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-54) The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")'s fabric covering ([kiswah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiswah "Kiswah")) is replaced annually in a formal ceremony.

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Kaaba-plan.svg/250px-Kaaba-plan.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kaaba-plan.svg)

A technical drawing of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") showing dimensions and elements

#### Hatim

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Hatim")]

Main article: [Hijr Ismail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijr_Ismail "Hijr Ismail")

Adjacent to the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") is the [Hijr Ismail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijr_Ismail "Hijr Ismail"), also known as the Hatim, a low semi-circular wall that marks an area historically regarded as part of the original footprint of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-55)

#### Black Stone

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Black Stone")]

Main article: [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/The_Blackstone.jpg/250px-The_Blackstone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Blackstone.jpg)

The [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone") is seen through a portal in the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").

The [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone") is set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba's external wall. Historically and culturally venerated in Islamic tradition, the stone today exists as several fragments within a silver frame and is a focal point of devotion during _tawaf_.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-57)

### Mataf (Tawaf area)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Mataf (Tawaf area)")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg/250px-Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg)

The Mataf full of worshipers

The mataf is the open, circular, paved area immediately surrounding the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") where _tawaf_ (circumambulation) is performed. Over centuries the mataf has been enlarged and modernised, including multi-level and climate-controlled expansions to accommodate the large and growing numbers of pilgrims that visit during [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and throughout the year.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-Long16-58) Major 20th- and 21st-century Saudi expansion programmes substantially increased the mataf’s capacity.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:3-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:5-37)

### Maqam Ibrahim

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Maqam Ibrahim")]

Main article: [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Maqam_Ibrahim%2C_Makkah.jpg/250px-Maqam_Ibrahim%2C_Makkah.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Maqam_Ibrahim,_Makkah.jpg)

The enclosure of [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim") in _Mataf_ area

[Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim") is a small square stone associated in Islamic tradition with the [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham "Abraham") ([Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam")). It is displayed near the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") under a protective enclosure.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-59) According to Islamic tradition, the [imprint on the stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrosomatoglyph "Petrosomatoglyph") came from Abraham's feet.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-61) It is the only standing historic structure in the _Mataf_ area out of at least six other, which were removed to clear the area for the circumambulation (_tawaf_).[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-madainmataf-62)

### Safa and Marwa

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Safa and Marwa")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg/250px-Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg)

Mount Safa

[Safa and Marwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safa_and_Marwa "Safa and Marwa") are two small hills within the mosque precinct, connected by the enclosed al-Mas'a walkway, where pilgrims perform the _saʿī_ ritual during [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-AtoZ-63) The ritual commemorates [Hājar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam") ([Hagar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar "Hagar")), wife of [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham "Abraham") and mother of [Ismail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismael_in_Islam "Ismael in Islam"), who ran between the hills searching for water for her infant son.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:0-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:1-65) The area was historically separate but incorporated into Masjid al-Haram during 20th-century expansions.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:3-36)

### Zamzam Well

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Zamzam Well")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/%D8%A8%D8%A6%D8%B1_%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%B2%D9%85_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%AB%D8%B1%D9%8A.jpg/250px-%D8%A8%D8%A6%D8%B1_%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%B2%D9%85_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%AB%D8%B1%D9%8A.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D8%A8%D8%A6%D8%B1_%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%B2%D9%85_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%AB%D8%B1%D9%8A.jpg)

Mouth-piece of the Zamzam well from the Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques Architecture Museum[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-Madaintwomosques-66)

The [Zamzam well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"), located 20 m (66 ft) east of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba"),[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-survey-67) is an ancient groundwater source traditionally linked to [Hājar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam") and [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael "Ishmael").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-islamonline-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:22-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:4-70) Modern engineering has enclosed the well and provides Zamzam water to pilgrims through pumping, bottling and distribution systems.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-71)

## Destruction of heritage sites

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Destruction of heritage sites")]

Main article: [Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia")

There has been some controversy that the expansion projects of the mosque and Mecca itself are causing harm to early Islamic heritage. Many ancient buildings, some more than a thousand years old, have been demolished to make room for the expansion.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-73)

**Masjid al-Haram** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): المسجد الحرام, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-Masjid al-Ḥarām_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'The Sacred Mosque'),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-4) also known as the **Great Mosque of Mecca**,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-5) is a [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") in Mecca, [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), serving as the holiest and most important mosque in [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-7)As of 2026,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit) the Great Mosque is the [largest mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_mosques "List of largest mosques") in the world.

The Great Mosque is considered, alongside the [Quba Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quba_Mosque "Quba Mosque") in [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), among the earliest mosques in Islam.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-8) According to Islamic scholars, Abraham is seen as having built the _Kaaba_ in Mecca, and consequently its sanctuary, which according to the Muslim view is seen as the first mosque[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-Palmer20163-9) that ever existed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-12)

It has undergone major renovations and expansions through the years.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-13) It has passed through the control of various [caliphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphs "Caliphs"), [sultans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sultans_of_the_Ottoman_Empire "List of sultans of the Ottoman Empire") and kings, and is now under the control of the [King of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Saudi_Arabia "King of Saudi Arabia") who is titled the [Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custodian_of_the_Two_Holy_Mosques "Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-14)

It encloses the vicinity of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca, in the [western region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz") of the country. It is among the pilgrimage sites associated with the [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj"), which every [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") according to orthodox Islamic belief, must perform at least once in their lives if able. It is also the main site for the performance of ʿ[Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah"), the lesser pilgrimage that can be undertaken any time of the year. The rites of both pilgrimages include [circumambulating the Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawaf "Tawaf") within the mosque. The Great Mosque contains other important sites, such as the [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone"), the [Zamzam Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"), [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim"), and the hills of [Safa and Marwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safa_and_Marwa "Safa and Marwa").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-15)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Further information: [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), [History of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Islam "History of Islam"), [History of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia "History of Saudi Arabia"), and [Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_architecture "Islamic architecture")

In the [pre-Islamic religions of Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_pre-Islamic_Arabia "Religion in pre-Islamic Arabia") -spanning from the [Levant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levant "Levant") to [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"), [numerous deities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_pre-Islamic_Arabian_deities "List of pre-Islamic Arabian deities") —such as, [Al-Lat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Lat "Al-Lat"), [Dhu al-Khalasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Khalasa "Dhu al-Khalasa"), and [al-Uzza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Uzza "Al-Uzza") (also occasionally referred to as [Chaabou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaabou "Chaabou")), [Dushara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dushara "Dushara"), [Dhu Samawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_Samawi "Dhu Samawi") etc.— were represented by [aniconic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aniconism "Aniconism") cubic stone carvings or by cubic structures regarded as [the abodes of these deities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaabas "Kaabas"); furthermore, the existence of "sacred/haram zones" surrounding these sanctuaries and the widespread use of [the name "Ka'b"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ka'b "Ka'b") to denote such sanctity, is well-established.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-16) Although the cultural heritage of the pagan era was largely eradicated during Islam's struggle to establish [Islamic monotheism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawhid "Tawhid"), historical research has uncovered traces of some [sanctuaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctuary "Sanctuary") that were significant enough to rival the Kaaba in Mecca; nevertheless, the belief that there has always been only one Kaaba has become deeply ingrained in Muslim literary and religious tradition. Today, the Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca are identified as the direction of prayer; however, an archaeological document found in the [Taif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif") region suggests that this view is anachronistic from the perspective of traditional Islamic historiography, as a stone inscription discovered there dates the construction of the Masjid al-Haram to the year 78 AH.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-17) Furthermore, a Quranic verse recounting [Muhammad's night journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra'_and_Mi'raj "Isra' and Mi'raj") —an event often presented today as a miracle— to the [Masjid al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Aqsa "Masjid al-Aqsa") offers clues suggesting that the *Masjid al-Haram* mentioned in the Quran might differ from the one located in Mecca. [Surah Al-Isra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Isra "Al-Isra")[17:1](https://quran.com/17?startingVerse=1):

> Glory be to the One Who took His servant by night from Masjid al-Haram to the [Masjid al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa_Mosque "Al-Aqsa Mosque") whose surroundings We have blessed, so that We may show him some of Our signs. Indeed, He alone is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing

The significance of mosque structures from the early Islamic period that face in different directions continues to be a subject of serious debate between [revisionist historians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revisionist_school_of_Islamic_studies "Revisionist school of Islamic studies") and conservatives.

### Era of Abraham and Ishmael

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Era of Abraham and Ishmael")]

See also: [Abraham in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam"), [Hagar in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam"), and [Ishmael in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael_in_Islam "Ishmael in Islam")

According to Islamic tradition in the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran"), [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam"), together with his son [Ismael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael_in_Islam "Ishmael in Islam"), raised the foundations of a house,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-18) which has been identified by commentators as the Kaaba. According to Islamic tradition, it is said that Allah showed Abraham the exact site, which was previously built by [Adam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_in_Islam "Adam in Islam"), very near to what is now the [Well of Zamzam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well_of_Zamzam "Well of Zamzam"). After Abraham had built the Kaaba, an angel is said to have brought him the [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone"), a celestial stone that, according to tradition, had fallen from Heaven on the nearby hill [Abu Qubays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Qubays_(mountain) "Abu Qubays (mountain)"). The Black Stone is believed by Islamic scholars to be the only remnant of the original structure made by Abraham.

After placing the Black Stone in the Eastern corner of the Kaaba, Abraham reportedly received a revelation in which God told the aged prophet that he should now go and proclaim the pilgrimage to mankind, so that men may come both from Arabia and from lands far away, on camel and on foot.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-19)

### Era of Muhammad

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Era of Muhammad")]

Main article: [Muhammad in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam")

Upon Muhammad's [victorious return to Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca") in 630 [CE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era"), he and a number of the _[Sahaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahaba "Sahaba")_ including Ali broke the idols in and around the Kaaba,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-20) similar to what, according to the Quran, Abraham did in his homeland. This ended polytheistic use of the Kaaba, and began monotheistic rule over it and its sanctuary.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-24)

### Rashidun era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rashidun era")]

The mosque has been expanded by [caliph Umar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar "Umar") in 637 CE by 1,500 m 2, in response to the increasing number of Muslims, its area has reached a total of 3,600 m 2, another expansion was carried out by [caliph Uthman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthman "Uthman") where the covered porticoes have been introduced for the first time.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:7-25)

### Umayyad era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Umayyad era")]

In 682, the ruler of Mecca [Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr"), who opposed the Umayyads following the death of [Mu'awiya I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu'awiya_I "Mu'awiya I") carried an expansion that increased the total area to 7,465 m 2,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:7-25) and following [the reconquest of Mecca by the Umayyads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mecca_(692) "Siege of Mecca (692)") in 692, the first major renovation to the mosque took place on the orders of [Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Malik_ibn_Marwan "Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-26) Before this renovation, which included the mosque's outer walls being raised, the mosque was a small open area with the Kaaba at the center. By the end of the 8th century, the mosque's old wooden columns had been replaced with marble columns and the wings of the prayer hall had been extended on both sides along with the addition of a [minaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret") on the orders of [Al-Walid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Walid_I "Al-Walid I").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-28)

### Abbasid era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Abbasid era")]

The next expansion of the mosque was sponsored by the [Abbasid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") caliph [al-Mansur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mansur "Al-Mansur") between 754 and 757.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:16-29) This was followed by a major expansion begun by his successor, Caliph [al-Mahdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mahdi "Al-Mahdi"), in 779. This work was completed shortly after him by his successor, Caliph [al-Hadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Hadi "Al-Hadi") (r.785–786),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:6-30) which made the made the mosque's total area to reach 28,000 m 2, this was the largest expansion to the size of the mosque until the Saudi era,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:7-25) except for two further extensions by the caliph [al-Mu'tadid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mu'tadid "Al-Mu'tadid") in 894–5 and by the caliph [al-Muqtadir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Muqtadir "Al-Muqtadir") in 918,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:6-30) but it retained its overall form from this period until the later [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") renovations.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:16-29)

### Ottoman era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Ottoman era")]

In 1570, [Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Sultan "Ottoman Sultan")[Selim II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selim_II "Selim II") commissioned the chief architect [Mimar Sinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimar_Sinan "Mimar Sinan") to renovate the mosque. This renovation resulted in the replacement of the flat roof with domes decorated with [calligraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calligraphy "Islamic calligraphy") internally, and the placement of new support columns which are acknowledged as the earliest architectural features of the present mosque. These features are the oldest surviving parts of the building.

During heavy rains and flash floods in 1621 and 1629, the walls of the Kaaba and the mosque suffered extensive damage.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-31) In 1629, during the reign of Sultan [Murad IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_IV "Murad IV"), the mosque was renovated. In the renovation of the mosque, a new stone arcade was added, three more minarets (bringing the total to seven) were built, and the marble flooring was retiled. This was the unaltered state of the mosque for nearly three centuries, the Ottoman era renovations did not expand the size of the mosque.

### The Saudi era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The Saudi era")]

#### First Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: First Saudi expansion")]

The first major renovation under the Saudi kings was done between 1955 and 1976. In this renovation, four more minarets were added, the ceiling was refurnished, and the floor was replaced with artificial stone and marble. The Mas'a gallery (As-Safa and Al-Marwah) is included in the Mosque, via roofing and enclosures. During this renovation many of the historical features built by the Ottomans, particularly the support columns, were [demolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia").

On 20 November 1979, the Great Mosque was [seized by extremist insurgents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure "Grand Mosque seizure") who called for the overthrow of the Saudi dynasty. They took hostages and in the ensuing siege hundreds were killed. These events came as a shock to the Islamic world, as violence is strictly forbidden within the mosque.

#### Second Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Second Saudi expansion")]

The second Saudi renovations under [King Fahd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Fahd "King Fahd"), added a new wing and an outdoor prayer area to the mosque. The new wing, which is also for prayers, is reached through the King Fahd Gate. This extension was performed between 1986 and 1994.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-32)

1987 to 2005 saw the building of more minarets, the erecting of a [King's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Saudi_Arabia "King of Saudi Arabia") residence overlooking the mosque and more prayer area in and around the mosque itself. These developments took place simultaneously with those in [Arafat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Arafat "Mount Arafat"), [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina,_Saudi_Arabia "Mina, Saudi Arabia") and [Muzdalifah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muzdalifah "Muzdalifah"). This extension also added 18 more gates, three domes corresponding in position to each gate and the installation of nearly 500 marble columns. Other modern developments added heated floors, air conditioning, escalators and a drainage system.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In addition, the King Fahd expansion includes 6 dedicated prayer halls for people with disabilities. These halls have ramps to facilitate entry and exit with wheelchairs, as well as dedicated paths and free electric and manual carts for their use.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-33)

#### Third Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Third Saudi expansion")]

In 2008, the Saudi government under [King Abdullah Ibn Abdulaziz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia "Abdullah of Saudi Arabia") announced an expansion[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-34) of the mosque, involving the [expropriation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expropriation "Expropriation") of land to the north and northwest of the mosque covering 300,000 m 2 (3,200,000 sq ft). At that time, the mosque covered an area of 356,800 m 2 (3,841,000 sq ft) including indoor and outdoor praying spaces. 40 billion riyals (US$10.6 billion) was allocated for the expansion project.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-35) In August 2011, the government under [King Abdullah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia "Abdullah of Saudi Arabia") announced further details of the expansion. It would cover an area of 400,000 m 2 (4,300,000 ft 2) and accommodate 1.2 million worshippers, including a multi-level extension on the north side of the complex, new stairways and tunnels, a gate named after King Abdullah, and two minarets, bringing the total number of minarets to eleven. The circumambulation areas (Mataf) around the Kaaba would be expanded and all closed spaces receive air conditioning. After completion, it would raise the mosque's capacity from 770,000 to over 2.5 million worshippers.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:3-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:5-37)[His successor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_kings_of_Saudi_Arabia "List of kings of Saudi Arabia"), [King Salman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia "Salman of Saudi Arabia") launched five megaprojects as part of the overall King Abdullah Expansion Project in July 2015, covering an area of 456,000 m 2 (4,910,000 sq ft). The project was carried out by the [Saudi Binladin Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Binladin_Group "Saudi Binladin Group").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-38) In 2012, the [Abraj Al Bait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraj_Al_Bait "Abraj Al Bait") complex was completed along with the 601-meter-tall (1,972 ft) Makkah Royal Clock Tower. Austrian company Lights of Vienna was hired to complete a 100 million euro order of 4700 chandeliers and light fixtures in 26 sizes in 2013. The chandeliers and light fixtures were installed in the Shamiya Extension of the mosque. Some of the biggest gilded chandeliers were priced at 1 million euros each. The company has since been the provider of additional light fixtures to the mosque and other buildings in Mecca.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-39) In 2025, the lighting for the Mataf extension was completed by Lights of Vienna. The project involved the delivery of 10 different lighting types and a total of around 550 custom-made chandeliers and luminaires, all produced from high-grade stainless steel and gilded with more than 200 kg of 24-karat gold. The project value is approximately €90 million. Part of the new lights was the 7-metre _Al Fath Gate Chandelier_, an octagonal, gold-plated chandelier with a 7-meter diameter and 360,000 lumens of output. All fixtures incorporate high-efficiency LED systems.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-41)

On 11 September 2015, at least 111 people died and 394 were injured [when a crane collapsed onto the mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_crane_collapse "Mecca crane collapse").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-46) Construction work was suspended after the incident, and remained on hold due to financial issues during the [2010s oil glut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010s_oil_glut "2010s oil glut"). Development was eventually restarted two years later in September 2017.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-47)

#### COVID-19 Pandemic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: COVID-19 Pandemic")]

On 5 March 2020, during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the mosque began to be closed at night and the Umrah pilgrimage was suspended to limit attendance.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-48) The resumption of Umrah service began on 4 October 2020 with the first phase of a gradual resumption that was limited to Saudi citizens and expatriates from within the Kingdom at a rate of 30 percent.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-49) Only 10,000 people were given Hajj visas in 2020 while 60,000 people were given visas in 2021.

## Pilgrimage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Pilgrimage")]

Main articles: [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah")

The Great Mosque is the main setting for the Hajj and Umrah pilgrimages[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-50) that occur in the month of [Dhu al-Hijja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Hijja "Dhu al-Hijja") in the [Islamic calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar "Islamic calendar") and at any time of the year, respectively. The Hajj pilgrimage is one of the Pillars of Islam, required of all able-bodied Muslims who can afford the trip. In recent times, over 5 million Muslims perform the Hajj every year.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-51)

## Notable structures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Notable structures")]

### Kaaba

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Kaaba")]

Main article: [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah%2C_Saudi_Arabia_%2852501405646%29.jpg/250px-The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah%2C_Saudi_Arabia_%2852501405646%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah,_Saudi_Arabia_(52501405646).jpg)

The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")

The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") is a [cuboid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuboid "Cuboid")-shaped building in the centre of the Masjid al-Haram and is the [most sacred site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_significant_religious_sites#Islam "List of significant religious sites") in Islam.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-eoi317-52) It is the [qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla")_(direction of prayer)_ for [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") worldwide. It is the focal point of the [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah") rites. The [pilgrims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage "Pilgrimage") perform the _tawaf_ (circumambulation) around its exterior.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-eoi317-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-54) The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")'s fabric covering ([kiswah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiswah "Kiswah")) is replaced annually in a formal ceremony.

#### Hatim

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Hatim")]

Main article: [Hijr Ismail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijr_Ismail "Hijr Ismail")

Adjacent to the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") is the [Hijr Ismail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijr_Ismail "Hijr Ismail"), also known as the Hatim, a low semi-circular wall that marks an area historically regarded as part of the original footprint of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-55)

#### Black Stone

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Black Stone")]

Main article: [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/The_Blackstone.jpg/250px-The_Blackstone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Blackstone.jpg)

The [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone") is seen through a portal in the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").

The [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone") is set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba's external wall. Historically and culturally venerated in Islamic tradition, the stone today exists as several fragments within a silver frame and is a focal point of devotion during _tawaf_.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-57)

### Mataf (Tawaf area)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Mataf (Tawaf area)")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg/250px-Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg)

The Mataf full of worshipers

The mataf is the open, circular, paved area immediately surrounding the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") where _tawaf_ (circumambulation) is performed. Over centuries the mataf has been enlarged and modernised, including multi-level and climate-controlled expansions to accommodate the large and growing numbers of pilgrims that visit during [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and throughout the year.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-Long16-58) Major 20th- and 21st-century Saudi expansion programmes substantially increased the mataf’s capacity.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:3-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:5-37)

### Maqam Ibrahim

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Maqam Ibrahim")]

Main article: [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Maqam_Ibrahim%2C_Makkah.jpg/250px-Maqam_Ibrahim%2C_Makkah.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Maqam_Ibrahim,_Makkah.jpg)

The enclosure of [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim") in _Mataf_ area

[Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim") is a small square stone associated in Islamic tradition with the [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham "Abraham") ([Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam")). It is displayed near the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") under a protective enclosure.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-59) According to Islamic tradition, the [imprint on the stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrosomatoglyph "Petrosomatoglyph") came from Abraham's feet.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-61) It is the only standing historic structure in the _Mataf_ area out of at least six other, which were removed to clear the area for the circumambulation (_tawaf_).[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-madainmataf-62)

### Safa and Marwa

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Safa and Marwa")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg/250px-Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg)

Mount Safa

[Safa and Marwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safa_and_Marwa "Safa and Marwa") are two small hills within the mosque precinct, connected by the enclosed al-Mas'a walkway, where pilgrims perform the _saʿī_ ritual during [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-AtoZ-63) The ritual commemorates [Hājar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam") ([Hagar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar "Hagar")), wife of [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham "Abraham") and mother of [Ismail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismael_in_Islam "Ismael in Islam"), who ran between the hills searching for water for her infant son.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:0-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:1-65) The area was historically separate but incorporated into Masjid al-Haram during 20th-century expansions.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:3-36)

### Zamzam Well

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Zamzam Well")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/%D8%A8%D8%A6%D8%B1_%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%B2%D9%85_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%AB%D8%B1%D9%8A.jpg/250px-%D8%A8%D8%A6%D8%B1_%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%B2%D9%85_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%AB%D8%B1%D9%8A.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D8%A8%D8%A6%D8%B1_%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%B2%D9%85_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%AB%D8%B1%D9%8A.jpg)

Mouth-piece of the Zamzam well from the Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques Architecture Museum[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-Madaintwomosques-66)

The [Zamzam well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"), located 20 m (66 ft) east of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba"),[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-survey-67) is an ancient groundwater source traditionally linked to [Hājar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam") and [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael "Ishmael").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-islamonline-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:22-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-:4-70) Modern engineering has enclosed the well and provides Zamzam water to pilgrims through pumping, bottling and distribution systems.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-71)

## Destruction of heritage sites

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Destruction of heritage sites")]

Main article: [Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia")

There has been some controversy that the expansion projects of the mosque and Mecca itself are causing harm to early Islamic heritage. Many ancient buildings, some more than a thousand years old, have been demolished to make room for the expansion.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca#cite_note-73)

The **Prophet's Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): ٱلْمَسْجِد ٱلنَّبَوِي, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-Masjid al-Nabawī_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'Mosque of the Prophet') is the [second mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_oldest_mosques "List of the oldest mosques") built by the Islamic prophet [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam") in [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), after the [Quba Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quba_Mosque "Quba Mosque"), as well as the second [largest mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_large_mosques "List of large mosques") and [holiest site in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiest_sites_in_Islam "Holiest sites in Islam"), after the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, in the [Saudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") region of the [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-2) The mosque is located at the heart of Medina, and is a major site of [pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziyarat "Ziyarat") that falls under the [purview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purview "Purview") of the [Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custodian_of_the_Two_Holy_Mosques "Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques").

[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") himself was involved in the construction of the mosque. At the time, the mosque's land belonged to two young orphans, Sahl and Suhayl, and when they learned that Muhammad wished to acquire their land to build a mosque, they went to Muhammad and offered the land to him as a gift; Muhammad insisted on paying a price for the land because they were orphaned children. The price agreed upon was paid by [Abu Ayyub al-Ansari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Ayyub_al-Ansari "Abu Ayyub al-Ansari"), who thus became the endower or donor (Arabic: وَاقِف, romanized:_wāqif_) of the mosque, on behalf or in favor of Muhammad.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-3)

Originally an open-air building, the mosque served as a community center, a court of law, and a religious school. It contained a raised platform or pulpit (_[minbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minbar "Minbar")_) for the people who taught the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") and for Muhammad to give the Friday sermon (_[khutbah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khutbah "Khutbah")_). Subsequent Islamic rulers greatly expanded and decorated the mosque, naming its walls, doors and minarets after themselves and their forefathers. After an expansion during the reign of the [Umayyad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate "Umayyad Caliphate") caliph [al-Walid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Walid_I "Al-Walid I") (r.705–715), it now incorporates the final resting place of Muhammad and the first two [Rashidun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate "Rashidun Caliphate") caliphs [Abu Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Bakr "Abu Bakr") (r.632–634) and [Umar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar "Umar") (r.634–644).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-Syed-4) One of the most notable features of the site is the [Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome") in the south-east corner of the mosque,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-Peterson-5) which was built above the site of the former house of [Aisha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aisha "Aisha"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-Syed-4) where the graves of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and Omar are located.

In 1909, under the reign of [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire")[Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan "Sultan")[Abdul Hamid II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdul_Hamid_II "Abdul Hamid II"), it became the first place in the [Arabian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula") to be provided with electrical lights.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-6) From the 14th century, the mosque was guarded by [eunuchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunuch "Eunuch"), the last remaining guardians were photographed at the request of then-[Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud#Third_Saudi_state "House of Saud")[Faisal bin Salman Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Salman_Al_Saud "Faisal bin Salman Al Saud"), and in 2015, only five were left.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-8) It is generally open regardless of date or time, and has only been closed to visitors once in modern times, as Ramadan approached during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Saudi_Arabia "COVID-19 pandemic in Saudi Arabia") in 2020.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-9)

### Under Muhammad and the Rashidun (622–660)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Under Muhammad and the Rashidun (622–660)")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Hadith_Masjid_an-Nabawi_Calligraphy_1.png/250px-Hadith_Masjid_an-Nabawi_Calligraphy_1.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hadith_Masjid_an-Nabawi_Calligraphy_1.png)

A [hadith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadith "Hadith") inscribed in the mosque which says "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers anywhere else, except for _Al-[Masjid al-Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid\_al-Haram "Masjid al-Haram")_."

The mosque was built by Muhammad in 622 after his arrival in Medina.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-10) Riding a camel called Qaswa, he arrived at the place where this mosque was built, which was being used as a burial ground.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200549-11) Refusing to accept the land as a gift from the two orphans, Sahl and Suhayl, who owned the land, he bought the land which was paid for by Abu Ayyub [al-Ansari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ansar_(Islam) "Ansar (Islam)"), and it took seven months to complete the construction of the mosque. It measured 30.5 m ×35.62 m (100.1 ft ×116.9 ft).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200549-11) The roof which was supported by palm trunks was made of beaten clay and palm leaves. It was at a height of 3.60 m (11.8 ft). The three doors of the mosque were the _Bāb ar-Raḥmah_ (بَاب ٱلرَّحْمَة, "Gate of the Mercy") to the south, _Bāb Jibrīl_ (بَاب جِبْرِيْل, "Gate of [Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel "Gabriel")") to the west, and _Bāb an-Nisāʾ_ (بَاب ٱلنِّسَاء, "Gate of the Women") to the east.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200549-11) At this time point in the history of the mosque, the wall of the _[qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla")_ was facing north to [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem"), and the [Suffah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffah "Suffah") was along the northern wall. In the year 7 AH, after the [Battle of Khaybar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Khaybar "Battle of Khaybar"), the mosque was expanded[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200550-12) to 47.32 m (155.2 ft) on each side, and three rows of columns were built beside the west wall, which became the place of praying.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200551-13) The mosque remained unaltered during the reign of Abu Bakr.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200551-13)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Al-Masjid_al-Nabaw%C4%AB_Original_Schematic_Plan_1_AH_622_CE_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AC%D8%AF_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%8A_%E2%80%94_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%B7_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%B5%D9%84%D9%8A.svg/250px-Al-Masjid_al-Nabaw%C4%AB_Original_Schematic_Plan_1_AH_622_CE_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AC%D8%AF_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%8A_%E2%80%94_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%B7_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%B5%D9%84%D9%8A.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Al-Masjid_al-Nabaw%C4%AB_Original_Schematic_Plan_1_AH_622_CE_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AC%D8%AF_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%8A_%E2%80%94_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%B7_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%B5%D9%84%D9%8A.svg)

A miniature of the mosque in 628 CE (7 AH) after the first expansion

Umar demolished all the houses around the mosque, except those of [Muhammad's wives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad's_wives "Muhammad's wives"), to expand it.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-14) The new mosque's dimensions became 57.49 m ×66.14 m (188.6 ft ×217.0 ft). Sun-dried mud bricks were used to construct the walls of the enclosure. Besides strewing pebbles on the floor, the roof's height was increased to 5.6 m (18 ft). Umar constructed three more gates for entrance. He also added _Al-Buṭayḥah_ (ٱلْبُطَيْحَة) for people to recite poetry.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200554-15)

The third Rashidun caliph [Uthman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthman "Uthman") demolished the mosque in 649. Ten months were spent in building the new rectangular shaped mosque whose face was turned towards the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca. The new mosque measured 81.40 m ×62.58 m (267.1 ft ×205.3 ft). The number of gates as well as their names remained the same.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200555-16) The enclosure was made of stones laid in mortar. The palm trunk columns were replaced by stone columns which were joined by iron clamps. [Teakwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teakwood "Teakwood") was used in reconstructing the ceiling filza.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200556-17)

### Umayyad era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Umayyad era")]

In 706 or 707, the [Umayyad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad "Umayyad") caliph [al-Walid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Walid_I "Al-Walid I") (r.705–715) instructed his governor of Medina, the future caliph [Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar_ibn_Abd_al-Aziz "Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz"), to significantly enlarge the mosque and carried out the fourth and most monumental expansion of the mosque.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:3-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillenbrand199473-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunt2014106-20) According to the architectural historian Robert Hillenbrand, the building of a large scale mosque in Medina, the original center of the caliphate, was an "acknowledgement" by al-Walid of "his own roots and those of Islam itself" and possibly an attempt to appease Medinan resentment at the loss of the city's political importance to [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilad_al-Sham "Bilad al-Sham") under the Umayyads.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillenbrand199473-19)

It took three years for the work to be completed. Raw materials were procured from the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-21) Al-Walid lavished large sums for the mosque's reconstruction and supplied mosaics and Greek and [Coptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copts "Copts") craftsmen.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBacharach199635-22) The area of the mosque was increased from the area 5,094 square metres (54,830 ft 2) of Uthman's time, to 8,672 square metres (93,340 ft 2).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200562-23) For the first time, [porticoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porticoes "Porticoes") were built in the mosque connecting the northern part of the structure to the sanctuary.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200562-23) The reconstruction preserved the location of the _qibla_ wall (in the direction of prayer), but Umar ordered the addition of a curved niche to it and this became the first concave [mihrab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihrab "Mihrab") in [Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_architecture "Islamic architecture").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:0523-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEttinghausenGrabarJenkins-Madina200124-25) The renovated mosque was richly decorated with marble paneling and mosaics covering its walls. Later written accounts, such as that of [Ibn Jubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Jubayr "Ibn Jubayr") (1184), described the mosaics as containing inscriptions and depicting landscapes with trees, suggesting that they resembled the style of contemporary Umayyad mosaics in the [Dome of the Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome_of_the_Rock "Dome of the Rock") in Jerusalem and the [Great Mosque of Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Damascus "Great Mosque of Damascus").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:24-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-27)

The mosque's redevelopment entailed the demolition of the living quarters of [Muhammad's wives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wives_of_Muhammad "Wives of Muhammad") and the expansion of the structure to incorporate the graves of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and Umar.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy2002127-28)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBacharach199635-22)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunt2014106%E2%80%93108-29) The vocal opposition to the demolition of Muhammad's home from local religious circles was dismissed by al-Walid.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillenbrand199473-19) A wall was built to segregate the mosque and the houses of the wives of Muhammad. The mosque was reconstructed in a trapezoid shape with the length of the longer side being 101.76 metres (333.9 ft).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200562-23)

According to the 10th-century writer [Ibn Rusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Rusta "Ibn Rusta"), [minarets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret") were also built for the first time during al-Walid's expansion as four towers were added to the mosque's corners.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom201349-30) They may be the first minarets in Islamic architecture,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEttinghausenGrabarJenkins-Madina200121-31) though it is not clear exactly what purpose these towers served in this early period.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom201349_(see_also_the_rest_of_this_chapter_for_context)-32) At the time of Ibn Rusta's writing, only one of the original four towers remained standing. The southwest minaret was demolished in 716 on the orders of [Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulayman_ibn_Abd_al-Malik "Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom201349-30)

### Abbasid era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Abbasid era")]

The [Abbasid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") caliph [al-Mahdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mahdi "Al-Mahdi") (r.775–785) extended the mosque to the north by 2,450 square metres (26,400 sq ft), the fifth expansion of the mosque which took four years to complete.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:3-18)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33) His name was also inscribed on the walls of the mosque. He also planned to remove six steps to the _minbar_, but abandoned this idea, fearing damage to the wooden platforms on which they were built.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunt2014116-34) The project required the demolition of the two northern minarets of al-Walid's time but they were replaced by two new towers at the northern corners of the new expansion.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom201349%E2%80%9350-35) According to an inscription of [Ibn Qutaybah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Qutaybah "Ibn Qutaybah"), the caliph [al-Ma'mun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ma'mun "Al-Ma'mun") (r.813–833) did "unspecified work" on the mosque. [Al-Mutawakkil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mutawakkil "Al-Mutawakkil") (r.847–861) lined the enclosure of Muhammad's tomb with marble.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunt2014118-36) In 1257–58 [Al-Musta'sim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Musta'sim "Al-Musta'sim") wanted to carry out a renovations program of the mosque but the renovation was interrupted by the [Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad "Siege of Baghdad").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33)

### Mamluk era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mamluk era")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Medina_Altes_Minaret_der_heiligen_Moschee%2C_erbaut_1483%3B_die_gr%C3%BCne_Kuppel_%C3%BCber_dem_Grabe_des_Propheten_erbaut_1840._1910._LCCN2002715728.jpg/250px-Medina_Altes_Minaret_der_heiligen_Moschee%2C_erbaut_1483%3B_die_gr%C3%BCne_Kuppel_%C3%BCber_dem_Grabe_des_Propheten_erbaut_1840._1910._LCCN2002715728.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Medina_Altes_Minaret_der_heiligen_Moschee,_erbaut_1483;_die_gr%C3%BCne_Kuppel_%C3%BCber_dem_Grabe_des_Propheten_erbaut_1840._1910._LCCN2002715728.jpg)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/The_Green_Dome%2C_Masjid_Nabawi%2C_Madina.jpg/250px-The_Green_Dome%2C_Masjid_Nabawi%2C_Madina.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Green_Dome,_Masjid_Nabawi,_Madina.jpg)

The Raisiyyah Minaret was built by Qaitbay in 1481 (886 AH). The [Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome") was originally built by Qalawun but was later rebuilt and painted green in 1837. Images in 1910 (left), and 2018 (right). The Green Dome is a defining symbol of the mosque.

In 1269, the [Mamluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamluk_Sultanate "Mamluk Sultanate") sultan [Baybars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baybars "Baybars") sent dozens of artisans led by the eunuch Emir Jamal al-Din Muhsin al-Salihi to rebuild the sanctuary, including enclosures around the tombs of Muhammad and of Fatima.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-37) in 1279 sultan [Qalawun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qalawun "Qalawun") added a wooden dome over the tomb of the prophet,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:1-38) and rebuilt the south-western minaret (Bab Al-Salam minaret) in 1307, which still retains its lower structure but with the upper section being built during the Ottoman era.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33)

In 1474 the Mamluk sultan [Qaitbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qaitbay "Qaitbay") ordered major renovation to be conducted on the mosque's roofs, columns, walls and minarets, the work also included the rebuilding of the wooden dome to a stone dome over the prophet's tomb in 1476.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:1-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-39) and in 1481–1483 he carried out the sixth expansion of the mosque,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:3-18) and ordered the reconstruction of the Nabawi mihrab, Uthmani Mirhab and the Tahajjud Mihrab. In addition, he rebuilt the south-eastern Raisiyyah Minaret (main minaret) in 1481. It was subsequently renovated in 1483 and again in 1486. He also commissioned the construction of the Western Minaret, which was later demolished during the Saudi expansions.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33)

### Ottoman era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Ottoman era")]
