**King Abdulaziz Medical City** (KAMC-Riyadh) is a medical complex in [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh"), [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia");[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:0-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:2-6) it was operated by the Ministry of National Guard Health Affairs. The complex developed from King Fahad National Guard Hospital,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:5-7) which opened in May 1983.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) In 2001, the National Guard Health Affairs reorganised its hospitals in Riyadh and Jeddah as King Absulaziz medical cities.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:3-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:4-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:6-11) King Fahad National Guard Hospital became part of the Riyadh-based King Abdulaziz medical city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:4-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:3-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:7-12)

KAMC-Riyadh provides primary, secondary, and tertiary healthcare services and includes a number of specialist hospitals and medical centres.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:8-13)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8)

It provides all types of care to all [Saudi National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_National_Guard "Saudi National Guard") soldiers and their families.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) In 2012, it became a recognized center on the international level in [conjoined twin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjoined_twin "Conjoined twin") separation surgery. It is the first center in the world with a 100% success rate in twin separation surgery.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-14)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The National Guard hospital in Riyadh was established in 1981,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:5-7) inaugurated as [King Fahad National Guard Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Fahad_National_Guard_Hospital?action=edit&redlink=1 "King Fahad National Guard Hospital (page does not exist)") in 1983 and began operations in May of that year.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:9-15) National Guard Health Affairs (NGHA) assumed responsibility for the hospital in 1994 and began programmes of modernisation, development, and expansion.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:9-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:8-13) KAMC-Riyadh's IVF unit was established in October 1995.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-17) In 2001, NGHA converted its hospitals in Riyadh and Jeddah into medical cities, under the name King Abdulaziz Medical City,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:3-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:4-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:6-11) with King Fahad National Guard Hospital becoming part of King Abdulaziz Medical City in Riyadh.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:4-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:3-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:7-12) In the same year, the first phase of the King Abdulaziz Cardiac Center was commissioned,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-18) and KAMC-Riyadh's Department of Surgery initiated a trauma registry to support injury surveillance and prevention.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-19)

The Long Term and Extended Care Centre was established adjacent to KAMC-Riyadh in May 2002 for patients requiring extended care.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:12-20) The Sleep Disorders Centre was established in 2003.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:13-21)

In January 2004, the College of Medicine at King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences (KSAU-HS) was established and was integrated within KAMC-Riyadh, with the medical city serving as its principal teaching centre.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-22) In September of the same year, the IVF clinic underwent expansion and renovation; it was subsequently known as the Division of Reproductive Medicine.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-23) The Rehabilitation Department was also expanded in 2004 with both occupational therapy and physiotherapy units. Medical Imaging, Laboratory, Pharmacy, and patients' wards also underwent development and renovation.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In December 2006, KAMC-Riyadh met the requirements for accreditation under [Joint Commission International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Commission "Joint Commission") (JCI) standards.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-24)

On 11 June 2011, NGHA inaugurated the Sheikh Sulaiman Al Rajhi Trauma Centre at KAMC-Riyadh, an expansion of the Cardiac Centre, and a blood bank building.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-26) The first phase of an expansion of the Emergency Care Centre opened in 2013, increasing capacity from 84 to 120 beds and adding adult and paediatric treatment areas.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-27)

King Abdullah Specialised Children's Hospital (KASCH) was opened in April 2015.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:11-28) It was formally inaugurated the following month by [King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia "Salman of Saudi Arabia")[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-29) as part of a group of new medical facilities at KAMC-Riyadh including the Central Laboratory building and the King Abdullah International Medical Research Centre.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:11-28)

During June-August 2015, KAMC-Riyadh experienced an outbreak of Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), which substantially disrupted hospital operations. On 18 August, the hospital was closed except for critical services.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-32) KAMC-Riyadh began resuming operations on 4 October 2015 following control of the outbreak and the completion of a development programme.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-35)

The Oncology and Haematology Centre was inaugrated on 5 January 2016. At its opening it included 40 outpatient clinics and 34 chemotherapy chairs.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:15-36)

The hospital is one of the centres used by the Saudi Conjoined Twins Program for conjoined-twin separation surgery.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-37)

## Facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Facilities")]

KAMC-Riyadh comprises multiple hospitals and specialised medical centres, King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences, and a research centre. The complex provides inpatient, outpatient, primary, tertiary, and specialised clinical services.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:10-38)

### Specialist hospitals and centres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Specialist hospitals and centres")]

King Abdullah Specialised Children's Hospital (KASCH), is a tertiary academic medical centre specialising in paediatric care.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:11-28) The adjacent Specialised Hospital for Women's Health is a 404-bed facility connected by a multi-storey bridge. Its services include obstetric, gynaecological, and neonatal care.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:14-39)

Other specialist facilities include the King Abdulaziz Cardiac Centre;[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) a specialist 150-bed cardiac facility with 45 intensive care beds,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-40) and the Hepatobiliary Sciences and Organ Transplant Centre, which provides liver and organ transplant services.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-41) The medical city also includes the Oncology and Haematology Centre.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:15-36)

### Emergency and critical care

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Emergency and critical care")]

KAMC-Riyadh meets Level I trauma centre criteria[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-42) and its trauma facilities include the Sheikh Sulaiman Al Rajhi Trauma Centre, inaugurated in June 2011,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-43) and an Adult Burn Centre with intensive care beds, an operating room, and outpatient clinics.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-44)

The complex also has six adult intensive care units (ICUs), including a neurological ICU, trauma ICU, surgical ICU, medical ICU, progressive care ICU, and respiratory ICU.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-45)

### Outpatient, primary and rehabilitative care

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Outpatient, primary and rehabilitative care")]

KAMC-Riyadh also provides dental and ambulatory (outpatient) care, long-term care/ rehabilitation, pharmaceutical care,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:0-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:2-6) and primary healthcare through a Riyadh network comprising four primary healthcare centres.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-46) The Long Term and Extended Care Centre provides care for patients requiring extended treatment.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:12-20)

KAMC-Riyadh also has accredited inpatient rehabilitation programmes, including an adult stroke specialty programme, and interdisciplinary rehabilitation programmes.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-47) The Sleep Disorders Centre provides in-laboratory [polysomnography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polysomnography "Polysomnography").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:13-21)

Other adult and paediatric services include: surgical and medical wards, [obstetrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstetrics "Obstetrics") and [gynaecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gynecology "Gynecology")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) (including labor and delivery units, an IVF clinic,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-48)[oncology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oncology "Oncology"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) antenatal and postpartum wards); paediatric oncology; an Ambulatory Care Center;[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) and a home health care program.

The medical city also contains operating facilities serving a range of specialties. The Ophthalmology Department serves both KAMC and KASCH and has three operating rooms in daily use,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-49) while dedicated orthopaedic operating rooms are assigned to adult orthopaedic, trauma, and spinal surgery.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-50)

### Pharmaceutical care

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Pharmaceutical care")]

The Department of Pharmaceutical Care operates a centralised pharmacy and 11 satellite pharmacies, seven serving inpatient areas and four serving outpatient areas. It also operates intravenous compounding facilities that prepare parenteral nutrition, chemotherapy, and other intravenous medications.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:10-38)

## Education and research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Education and research")]

The medical city is associated with King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences and includes the Colleges of Medicine and Nursing.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:14-39)

The wider Riyadh complex also includes the King Abdullah International Medical Research Centre (KAIMRC).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-51) Its research infrastructure includes the Saudi [Biobank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biobank "Biobank"), and [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") and cord-blood bank facilities.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-52)

**King Abdulaziz Medical City** (KAMC-Riyadh) is a medical complex in [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh"), [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia");[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:0-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:2-6) it was operated by the Ministry of National Guard Health Affairs. The complex developed from King Fahad National Guard Hospital,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:5-7) which opened in May 1983.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) In 2001, the National Guard Health Affairs reorganised its hospitals in Riyadh and Jeddah as King Absulaziz medical cities.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:3-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:4-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:6-11) King Fahad National Guard Hospital became part of the Riyadh-based King Abdulaziz medical city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:4-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:3-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:7-12)

KAMC-Riyadh provides primary, secondary, and tertiary healthcare services and includes a number of specialist hospitals and medical centres.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:8-13)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8)

It provides all types of care to all [Saudi National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_National_Guard "Saudi National Guard") soldiers and their families.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) In 2012, it became a recognized center on the international level in [conjoined twin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjoined_twin "Conjoined twin") separation surgery. It is the first center in the world with a 100% success rate in twin separation surgery.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-14)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The National Guard hospital in Riyadh was established in 1981,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:5-7) inaugurated as [King Fahad National Guard Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Fahad_National_Guard_Hospital?action=edit&redlink=1 "King Fahad National Guard Hospital (page does not exist)") in 1983 and began operations in May of that year.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:9-15) National Guard Health Affairs (NGHA) assumed responsibility for the hospital in 1994 and began programmes of modernisation, development, and expansion.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:9-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:8-13) KAMC-Riyadh's IVF unit was established in October 1995.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-17) In 2001, NGHA converted its hospitals in Riyadh and Jeddah into medical cities, under the name King Abdulaziz Medical City,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:3-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:4-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:6-11) with King Fahad National Guard Hospital becoming part of King Abdulaziz Medical City in Riyadh.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:4-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:3-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:7-12) In the same year, the first phase of the King Abdulaziz Cardiac Center was commissioned,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-18) and KAMC-Riyadh's Department of Surgery initiated a trauma registry to support injury surveillance and prevention.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-19)

The Long Term and Extended Care Centre was established adjacent to KAMC-Riyadh in May 2002 for patients requiring extended care.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:12-20) The Sleep Disorders Centre was established in 2003.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:13-21)

In January 2004, the College of Medicine at King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences (KSAU-HS) was established and was integrated within KAMC-Riyadh, with the medical city serving as its principal teaching centre.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-22) In September of the same year, the IVF clinic underwent expansion and renovation; it was subsequently known as the Division of Reproductive Medicine.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-23) The Rehabilitation Department was also expanded in 2004 with both occupational therapy and physiotherapy units. Medical Imaging, Laboratory, Pharmacy, and patients' wards also underwent development and renovation.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In December 2006, KAMC-Riyadh met the requirements for accreditation under [Joint Commission International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Commission "Joint Commission") (JCI) standards.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-24)

On 11 June 2011, NGHA inaugurated the Sheikh Sulaiman Al Rajhi Trauma Centre at KAMC-Riyadh, an expansion of the Cardiac Centre, and a blood bank building.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-26) The first phase of an expansion of the Emergency Care Centre opened in 2013, increasing capacity from 84 to 120 beds and adding adult and paediatric treatment areas.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-27)

King Abdullah Specialised Children's Hospital (KASCH) was opened in April 2015.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:11-28) It was formally inaugurated the following month by [King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia "Salman of Saudi Arabia")[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-29) as part of a group of new medical facilities at KAMC-Riyadh including the Central Laboratory building and the King Abdullah International Medical Research Centre.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:11-28)

During June-August 2015, KAMC-Riyadh experienced an outbreak of Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), which substantially disrupted hospital operations. On 18 August, the hospital was closed except for critical services.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-32) KAMC-Riyadh began resuming operations on 4 October 2015 following control of the outbreak and the completion of a development programme.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-35)

The Oncology and Haematology Centre was inaugrated on 5 January 2016. At its opening it included 40 outpatient clinics and 34 chemotherapy chairs.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:15-36)

The hospital is one of the centres used by the Saudi Conjoined Twins Program for conjoined-twin separation surgery.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-37)

## Facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Facilities")]

KAMC-Riyadh comprises multiple hospitals and specialised medical centres, King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences, and a research centre. The complex provides inpatient, outpatient, primary, tertiary, and specialised clinical services.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:10-38)

### Specialist hospitals and centres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Specialist hospitals and centres")]

King Abdullah Specialised Children's Hospital (KASCH), is a tertiary academic medical centre specialising in paediatric care.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:11-28) The adjacent Specialised Hospital for Women's Health is a 404-bed facility connected by a multi-storey bridge. Its services include obstetric, gynaecological, and neonatal care.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:14-39)

Other specialist facilities include the King Abdulaziz Cardiac Centre;[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) a specialist 150-bed cardiac facility with 45 intensive care beds,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-40) and the Hepatobiliary Sciences and Organ Transplant Centre, which provides liver and organ transplant services.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-41) The medical city also includes the Oncology and Haematology Centre.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:15-36)

### Emergency and critical care

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Emergency and critical care")]

KAMC-Riyadh meets Level I trauma centre criteria[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-42) and its trauma facilities include the Sheikh Sulaiman Al Rajhi Trauma Centre, inaugurated in June 2011,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-43) and an Adult Burn Centre with intensive care beds, an operating room, and outpatient clinics.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-44)

The complex also has six adult intensive care units (ICUs), including a neurological ICU, trauma ICU, surgical ICU, medical ICU, progressive care ICU, and respiratory ICU.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-45)

### Outpatient, primary and rehabilitative care

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Outpatient, primary and rehabilitative care")]

KAMC-Riyadh also provides dental and ambulatory (outpatient) care, long-term care/ rehabilitation, pharmaceutical care,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:0-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:2-6) and primary healthcare through a Riyadh network comprising four primary healthcare centres.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-46) The Long Term and Extended Care Centre provides care for patients requiring extended treatment.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:12-20)

KAMC-Riyadh also has accredited inpatient rehabilitation programmes, including an adult stroke specialty programme, and interdisciplinary rehabilitation programmes.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-47) The Sleep Disorders Centre provides in-laboratory [polysomnography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polysomnography "Polysomnography").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:13-21)

Other adult and paediatric services include: surgical and medical wards, [obstetrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstetrics "Obstetrics") and [gynaecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gynecology "Gynecology")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) (including labor and delivery units, an IVF clinic,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-48)[oncology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oncology "Oncology"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) antenatal and postpartum wards); paediatric oncology; an Ambulatory Care Center;[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:1-8) and a home health care program.

The medical city also contains operating facilities serving a range of specialties. The Ophthalmology Department serves both KAMC and KASCH and has three operating rooms in daily use,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-49) while dedicated orthopaedic operating rooms are assigned to adult orthopaedic, trauma, and spinal surgery.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-50)

### Pharmaceutical care

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Pharmaceutical care")]

The Department of Pharmaceutical Care operates a centralised pharmacy and 11 satellite pharmacies, seven serving inpatient areas and four serving outpatient areas. It also operates intravenous compounding facilities that prepare parenteral nutrition, chemotherapy, and other intravenous medications.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:10-38)

## Education and research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Education and research")]

The medical city is associated with King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences and includes the Colleges of Medicine and Nursing.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-:14-39)

The wider Riyadh complex also includes the King Abdullah International Medical Research Centre (KAIMRC).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-51) Its research infrastructure includes the Saudi [Biobank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biobank "Biobank"), and [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") and cord-blood bank facilities.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_Medical_City#cite_note-52)

The **King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Centre** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مستشفى الملك فيصل التخصصي ومركز الأبحاث) (KFSHRC) is a non-profit [tertiary healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_healthcare "Tertiary healthcare") institution headquartered in [Riyadh, Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh,_Saudi_Arabia "Riyadh, Saudi Arabia").

## Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

As a tertiary referral hospital, it offers primary and specialized inpatient and outpatient medical care and participates in clinical research studies. The hospital is known for providing treatments in [oncology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oncology "Oncology"), [organ transplantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_transplantation "Organ transplantation"), [cardiovascular medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_medicine "Cardiovascular medicine"), and [genomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genomics "Genomics").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-:0-1) In 2024, it was ranked 229th globally and 2nd in the Middle East by [Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

KFSHRC was established in 1970 by [King Faisal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_bin_Abdulaziz_Al_Saud "King Faisal bin Abdulaziz Al Saud") on land he donated for the hospital. The hospital was officially inaugurated in 1975 by [King Khalid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Khalid_bin_Abdulaziz "King Khalid bin Abdulaziz"). KFSHRC began operations, initially with a capacity of 17 beds.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-3)

The hospital established its Organ Transplant Program in 1981 when the first kidney transplant was performed at the institute.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-5) In 1984, KFSHRC performed its first [HSCT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hematopoietic_stem_cell_transplantation "Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation") and was the first HSCT center in the [World Health Organization Eastern Mediterranean Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WHO_Regional_Office_for_the_Eastern_Mediterranean "WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean") to perform the procedure.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-7) In 1989, the hospital conducted its first heart transplant.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-10)

From 1973 to 1985, the hospital was administered by the [Hospital Corporation of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_Corporation_of_America "Hospital Corporation of America") (HCA). In 1985, following a Royal Decree, the contract with HCA ended and the responsibility for the administration and operation of the hospital's premises was undertaken by a national team.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

During the 1990s, KFSHRC introduced new areas of healthcare, including a colorectal unit in 1990 and a national [home healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_health_care "Home health care") program in 1991.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-12) The outpatient building began operations in 1995. The King Fahd National Centre for Children's Cancer (KFNCCCR) at KFSHRC was established in 1997 to provide specialized care for [pediatric oncology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pediatric_oncology "Pediatric oncology") and hematology patients.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-14)

KFSHRC Jeddah was established in 2000.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-spa.gov.sa-15) By 2010, the first national [bone bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_bank "Bone bank") was established at KFSHRC. The King Abdullah Center for Oncology and Liver Diseases at KFSHRC Riyadh began operations in 2017, and KFSHRC's Madinah branch was added in 2019.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-16)

In 2020, the Centre for Genomic Medicine was for research and personalized treatment of genetic diseases.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-17) In 2021, KFSHRC was restructured into an independent, non-profit foundation through a Royal Decree, aligning with [Saudi Vision 2030](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Vision_2030 "Saudi Vision 2030") objectives.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-20)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Governance")]

Dr. Majid Ibrahim Alfayyadh is the CEO of KFSHRC. As of December 2023, the Board of Directors includes independent members and representatives from the Ministry of Health, Royal Clinics, and Ministry of Finance.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-21)

## Operations and facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Operations and facilities")]

The hospital operates three branches in Saudi Arabia, located in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Madinah. KFSHRC Riyadh serves as the primary facility. The branch, covers an area of 1,000,000m² and has a capacity of 1,519 beds. It serves as the primary KFSHRC health facility.

The Jeddah branch is a 500 bed hospital and serves the western region in Saudi Arabia. The Madinah branch has a 300 bed capacity.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-22)

In 2023, KFSHRC reported 1.9 million outpatient visits and an average patient stay of 8.8 days across its branches.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-spa.gov.sa-15)

## Specialized departments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Specialized departments")]

KFSHRC provides specialized programs and services in organ transplantation, oncology, genomics, and neuroscience.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-:0-1) Since the establishment of the Organ Transplant Program in 1981, KFSHRC has performed up to 9,000 successful organ transplants. Additionally, more than 5,000 kidneys have been transplanted since the center's inception.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-23)

In 2023, KFSHRC conducted the world’s first fully robotic liver transplant from a living donor.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-25) In 2024, the hospital performed the world’s first fully robotic heart transplant on a 16-year-old patient with end-stage heart failure.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-28)

The Oncology Centre treated approximately 25% of Saudi Arabia’s cancer cases in 2023.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-29) The Oncology Centre engages in research and development of treatments, such as [CAR T-cell therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAR_T-cell_therapy "CAR T-cell therapy") for blood cancers.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-30)

KFSHRC’s genomic medicine services include [whole genome sequencing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_genome_sequencing "Whole genome sequencing") for diagnostic accuracy and personalized treatment plans. By 2023, the hospital conducted over 7,000 sequencing tests, with accurate diagnoses achieved in over half of the cases.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-31)

## Research and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Research and education")]

The institute provides education and training programs, including postgraduate and undergraduate medical education in collaboration with universities in Saudi Arabia. It also operates a simulation center for training healthcare professionals.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-32)

KFSHRC collaborates with international and national institutions on research and education, including [Johns Hopkins Medicine International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_Medicine_International "Johns Hopkins Medicine International"), [Alfaisal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfaisal_University "Alfaisal University"), [Mayo Clinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayo_Clinic "Mayo Clinic"), [Massachusetts General Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_General_Hospital "Massachusetts General Hospital") and [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (MIT).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-35)

The **King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Centre** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مستشفى الملك فيصل التخصصي ومركز الأبحاث) (KFSHRC) is a non-profit [tertiary healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_healthcare "Tertiary healthcare") institution headquartered in [Riyadh, Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh,_Saudi_Arabia "Riyadh, Saudi Arabia").

## Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

As a tertiary referral hospital, it offers primary and specialized inpatient and outpatient medical care and participates in clinical research studies. The hospital is known for providing treatments in [oncology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oncology "Oncology"), [organ transplantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_transplantation "Organ transplantation"), [cardiovascular medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_medicine "Cardiovascular medicine"), and [genomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genomics "Genomics").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-:0-1) In 2024, it was ranked 229th globally and 2nd in the Middle East by [Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

KFSHRC was established in 1970 by [King Faisal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_bin_Abdulaziz_Al_Saud "King Faisal bin Abdulaziz Al Saud") on land he donated for the hospital. The hospital was officially inaugurated in 1975 by [King Khalid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Khalid_bin_Abdulaziz "King Khalid bin Abdulaziz"). KFSHRC began operations, initially with a capacity of 17 beds.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-3)

The hospital established its Organ Transplant Program in 1981 when the first kidney transplant was performed at the institute.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-5) In 1984, KFSHRC performed its first [HSCT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hematopoietic_stem_cell_transplantation "Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation") and was the first HSCT center in the [World Health Organization Eastern Mediterranean Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WHO_Regional_Office_for_the_Eastern_Mediterranean "WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean") to perform the procedure.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-7) In 1989, the hospital conducted its first heart transplant.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-10)

From 1973 to 1985, the hospital was administered by the [Hospital Corporation of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_Corporation_of_America "Hospital Corporation of America") (HCA). In 1985, following a Royal Decree, the contract with HCA ended and the responsibility for the administration and operation of the hospital's premises was undertaken by a national team.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

During the 1990s, KFSHRC introduced new areas of healthcare, including a colorectal unit in 1990 and a national [home healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_health_care "Home health care") program in 1991.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-12) The outpatient building began operations in 1995. The King Fahd National Centre for Children's Cancer (KFNCCCR) at KFSHRC was established in 1997 to provide specialized care for [pediatric oncology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pediatric_oncology "Pediatric oncology") and hematology patients.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-14)

KFSHRC Jeddah was established in 2000.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-spa.gov.sa-15) By 2010, the first national [bone bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_bank "Bone bank") was established at KFSHRC. The King Abdullah Center for Oncology and Liver Diseases at KFSHRC Riyadh began operations in 2017, and KFSHRC's Madinah branch was added in 2019.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-16)

In 2020, the Centre for Genomic Medicine was for research and personalized treatment of genetic diseases.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-17) In 2021, KFSHRC was restructured into an independent, non-profit foundation through a Royal Decree, aligning with [Saudi Vision 2030](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Vision_2030 "Saudi Vision 2030") objectives.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-20)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Governance")]

Dr. Majid Ibrahim Alfayyadh is the CEO of KFSHRC. As of December 2023, the Board of Directors includes independent members and representatives from the Ministry of Health, Royal Clinics, and Ministry of Finance.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-21)

## Operations and facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Operations and facilities")]

The hospital operates three branches in Saudi Arabia, located in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Madinah. KFSHRC Riyadh serves as the primary facility. The branch, covers an area of 1,000,000m² and has a capacity of 1,519 beds. It serves as the primary KFSHRC health facility.

The Jeddah branch is a 500 bed hospital and serves the western region in Saudi Arabia. The Madinah branch has a 300 bed capacity.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-22)

In 2023, KFSHRC reported 1.9 million outpatient visits and an average patient stay of 8.8 days across its branches.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-spa.gov.sa-15)

## Specialized departments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Specialized departments")]

KFSHRC provides specialized programs and services in organ transplantation, oncology, genomics, and neuroscience.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-:0-1) Since the establishment of the Organ Transplant Program in 1981, KFSHRC has performed up to 9,000 successful organ transplants. Additionally, more than 5,000 kidneys have been transplanted since the center's inception.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-23)

In 2023, KFSHRC conducted the world’s first fully robotic liver transplant from a living donor.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-25) In 2024, the hospital performed the world’s first fully robotic heart transplant on a 16-year-old patient with end-stage heart failure.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-28)

The Oncology Centre treated approximately 25% of Saudi Arabia’s cancer cases in 2023.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-29) The Oncology Centre engages in research and development of treatments, such as [CAR T-cell therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAR_T-cell_therapy "CAR T-cell therapy") for blood cancers.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-30)

KFSHRC’s genomic medicine services include [whole genome sequencing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_genome_sequencing "Whole genome sequencing") for diagnostic accuracy and personalized treatment plans. By 2023, the hospital conducted over 7,000 sequencing tests, with accurate diagnoses achieved in over half of the cases.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-31)

## Research and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Research and education")]

The institute provides education and training programs, including postgraduate and undergraduate medical education in collaboration with universities in Saudi Arabia. It also operates a simulation center for training healthcare professionals.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-32)

KFSHRC collaborates with international and national institutions on research and education, including [Johns Hopkins Medicine International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_Medicine_International "Johns Hopkins Medicine International"), [Alfaisal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfaisal_University "Alfaisal University"), [Mayo Clinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayo_Clinic "Mayo Clinic"), [Massachusetts General Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_General_Hospital "Massachusetts General Hospital") and [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (MIT).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Specialist_Hospital_and_Research_Centre#cite_note-35)

The **Al-Qantara Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مَسْجِد ٱلْقَنْطَرَة, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Masjid al-Qanṭarah_), also known as **Al-Madhoun Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مَسْجِد ٱلْمَدْهُوْن, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Masjid al-Madhūn_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-1) or **Qabil Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مَسْجِد قَابِل, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Masjid Qābil_), is an abandoned historical [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") from the [Ottoman era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_era "Ottoman era") in the neighbourhood of Al-Mathnah in the city of [At-Ta’if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif"), [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").

## Background and history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Qantara_Mosque&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and history")]

Built during the time of [Sharif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharif_of_Mecca "Sharif of Mecca")[Abd al-Muttalib ibn Ghalib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Muttalib_ibn_Ghalib "Abd al-Muttalib ibn Ghalib") in the 19th century,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-2) the mosque is believed to be constructed upon one of the sites where the [Islamic Prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_and_messengers_in_Islam "Prophets and messengers in Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam") and his adopted son, [Zayd ibn Harithah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayd_ibn_Haritha_al-Kalbi "Zayd ibn Haritha al-Kalbi"), took rest in an orchard while they were on their way back to Mecca, in the aftermath of their [expulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad's_visit_to_Ta'if "Muhammad's visit to Ta'if") by the leaders and residents of At-Ta’if around 620 [C.E.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era"), during the [Year of Sorrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_Sorrow "Year of Sorrow"). Pilgrims travelling to Mecca to perform [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah") often pay visits and offer prayers in the mosque.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-3)

After Taif's tribal leaders and residents rejected the message of [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"), they ordered their children to throw rock and stones at him and Zayd ibn Harithah. Both Muhammad and Zayd were badly injured and started bleeding as a result. Once outside the walls of Taif, Muhammad almost collapsed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-Restatement-4)

After travelling for a short distance, they stopped in an orchard that belonged to Utaba and Sheba. The owners of the [orchard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard "Orchard") had seen Muhammad being persecuted in Mecca and on this occasion they felt some sympathy toward their fellow townsman. The owners of the orchard sent a slave, named [Addas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addas "Addas"), a young [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") boy who took Muhammad into his hut, dressed his wounds, and let him rest and recuperate until he felt strong enough to resume his journey across the rough terrain between At-Ta’if and Mecca.

The mosque is said to have been constructed during the reign of [Sharif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharif_of_Mecca "Sharif of Mecca")[Abd al-Muttalib ibn Ghalib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Muttalib_ibn_Ghalib "Abd al-Muttalib ibn Ghalib") in mid-19th century, when Taif used to be part of the [Habesh Eyalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habesh_Eyalet "Habesh Eyalet") of the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"). It derives its name from the al-Madhoun mountain.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-5)

The **Al-Qantara Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مَسْجِد ٱلْقَنْطَرَة, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Masjid al-Qanṭarah_), also known as **Al-Madhoun Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مَسْجِد ٱلْمَدْهُوْن, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Masjid al-Madhūn_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-1) or **Qabil Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مَسْجِد قَابِل, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Masjid Qābil_), is an abandoned historical [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") from the [Ottoman era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_era "Ottoman era") in the neighbourhood of Al-Mathnah in the city of [At-Ta’if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif"), [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").

## Background and history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Qantara_Mosque&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and history")]

Built during the time of [Sharif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharif_of_Mecca "Sharif of Mecca")[Abd al-Muttalib ibn Ghalib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Muttalib_ibn_Ghalib "Abd al-Muttalib ibn Ghalib") in the 19th century,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-2) the mosque is believed to be constructed upon one of the sites where the [Islamic Prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_and_messengers_in_Islam "Prophets and messengers in Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam") and his adopted son, [Zayd ibn Harithah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayd_ibn_Haritha_al-Kalbi "Zayd ibn Haritha al-Kalbi"), took rest in an orchard while they were on their way back to Mecca, in the aftermath of their [expulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad's_visit_to_Ta'if "Muhammad's visit to Ta'if") by the leaders and residents of At-Ta’if around 620 [C.E.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era"), during the [Year of Sorrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_Sorrow "Year of Sorrow"). Pilgrims travelling to Mecca to perform [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah") often pay visits and offer prayers in the mosque.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-3)

After Taif's tribal leaders and residents rejected the message of [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"), they ordered their children to throw rock and stones at him and Zayd ibn Harithah. Both Muhammad and Zayd were badly injured and started bleeding as a result. Once outside the walls of Taif, Muhammad almost collapsed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-Restatement-4)

After travelling for a short distance, they stopped in an orchard that belonged to Utaba and Sheba. The owners of the [orchard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard "Orchard") had seen Muhammad being persecuted in Mecca and on this occasion they felt some sympathy toward their fellow townsman. The owners of the orchard sent a slave, named [Addas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addas "Addas"), a young [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") boy who took Muhammad into his hut, dressed his wounds, and let him rest and recuperate until he felt strong enough to resume his journey across the rough terrain between At-Ta’if and Mecca.

The mosque is said to have been constructed during the reign of [Sharif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharif_of_Mecca "Sharif of Mecca")[Abd al-Muttalib ibn Ghalib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Muttalib_ibn_Ghalib "Abd al-Muttalib ibn Ghalib") in mid-19th century, when Taif used to be part of the [Habesh Eyalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habesh_Eyalet "Habesh Eyalet") of the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"). It derives its name from the al-Madhoun mountain.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qantara_Mosque#cite_note-5)

**Al-Rayah Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مسجد الراية) was one of the historic mosques located in the Al-Judariyyah district of Mecca, [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-1)

## Name

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Name")]

The [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") was given this name because it was built on the spot where the Prophet [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") planted his banner on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, which took place in Ramadan of the 8th year after Hijrah.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

*   The mosque was originally built after the [Conquest of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-4)
*   During the Abbasid era, in 640 AH, the mosque was rebuilt.
*   In 1431 AH, the authorities decided to demolish Al-Rayah Mosque as part of the northern expansion project of the Grand Mosque, aimed at accommodating the increasing numbers of pilgrims and visitors.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-5)

## Significance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Significance")]

The mosque held historical importance connected to the memory of the Islamic conquest and the early development of Mecca.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-6)

*   It was an important symbol marking the place where the Prophet raised the banner of the Muslims upon entering Makkah.
*   Given its close proximity to the Grand Mosque, the site carried spiritual and historical value.
*   The mosque was removed to facilitate the Masjid al-Haram expansion project, which was carried out to better serve pilgrims.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-7)

**Al-Rayah Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مسجد الراية) was one of the historic mosques located in the Al-Judariyyah district of Mecca, [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-1)

## Name

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Name")]

The [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") was given this name because it was built on the spot where the Prophet [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") planted his banner on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, which took place in Ramadan of the 8th year after Hijrah.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

*   The mosque was originally built after the [Conquest of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-4)
*   During the Abbasid era, in 640 AH, the mosque was rebuilt.
*   In 1431 AH, the authorities decided to demolish Al-Rayah Mosque as part of the northern expansion project of the Grand Mosque, aimed at accommodating the increasing numbers of pilgrims and visitors.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-5)

## Significance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Significance")]

The mosque held historical importance connected to the memory of the Islamic conquest and the early development of Mecca.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-6)

*   It was an important symbol marking the place where the Prophet raised the banner of the Muslims upon entering Makkah.
*   Given its close proximity to the Grand Mosque, the site carried spiritual and historical value.
*   The mosque was removed to facilitate the Masjid al-Haram expansion project, which was carried out to better serve pilgrims.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Rayah_Mosque,_Mecca#cite_note-7)
