The **Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): جَامِع ٱلشَّيْخ زَايِد ٱلْكَبِيْر _Jāmiʿ Aš-Šaykh Zāyid Al-Kabīr_) is a mosque located in [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"), the capital city of the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1) It is the [country's largest mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mosques_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "List of mosques in the United Arab Emirates"), and is the key place of worship for [daily Islamic prayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salah "Salah"). There is a [smaller replica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque,_Solo "Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, Solo") of this mosque in [Surakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surakarta "Surakarta"), a city in [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-TheNational_11-2022-2)

The Grand Mosque was constructed between 1994 and 2007 and was inaugurated in December 2007.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-3) The building complex measures approximately 290 by 420 m (950 by 1,380 ft), covering an area of more than 12 hectares (30 acres), excluding exterior landscaping and vehicle parking. The main axis of the building is rotated about 12° south of true west, aligning it in the direction of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca, [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").

The project was launched by the late president of the U.A.E., [Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh "Sheikh")[Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_bin_Sultan_Al_Nahyan "Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan"), who wanted to establish a structure that would unite the cultural diversity of the Islamic world with the historical and modern values of architecture and art.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-4) In 2004, Sheikh Zayed died and was buried in the courtyard of the mosque.

Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque Center (SZGMC) offices are located in the west [minarets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret"). SZGMC manages the day-to-day operations and serves as a center of learning and discovery through its educational cultural activities and visitor programs. The library, located in the northeast minaret, serves the community with classic books and publications addressing a range of Islamic subjects: [sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_in_the_medieval_Islamic_world "Science in the medieval Islamic world"), [civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Golden_Age "Islamic Golden Age"), [calligraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calligraphy "Islamic calligraphy"), the [arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_art "Islamic art"), and coins, including some rare publications. The collection comprises material in a broad range of languages, including Arabic, English, French, Italian, Spanish, German, and Korean. For two years running, it was voted the world's second favourite landmark by [TripAdvisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TripAdvisor "TripAdvisor").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-5)

The Grand Mosque has been a significant destination for visiting foreign leaders during official state visits to the [UAE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"). Notable visitors include [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-6) the then US Vice President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-7) Australian Prime Minister [Anthony Albanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Albanese "Anthony Albanese").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-8) and Indian Prime Minister [Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-9)

## Design and construction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Design and construction")]

The mosque was built under the guidance and supervision of Sheikh Zayed, who was buried here after his death in 2004. It features 82 domes, more than 1,000 columns, 24-carat-gold gilded chandeliers and the world's largest hand-knotted carpet. The main prayer hall is dominated by one of the largest chandeliers. The mosque was designed under the management of the [Syrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrians "Syrians") architect Youssef Abdelke, and three other architectural designers from [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria") who completed the design and worked on developing it, Basem Barghouti, Moataz Al-Halabi, and Imad Malas.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-10)

The mosque's architect Yusef Abdelki took inspiration from a number of sources: the [Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_al-Abbas_al-Mursi_Mosque "Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi Mosque") in [Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria "Alexandria"), designed by [Mario Rossi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Rossi_(architect) "Mario Rossi (architect)") in the 1920s;[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-11) the [Badshahi Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badshahi_Mosque "Badshahi Mosque") in [Lahore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore "Lahore"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan");[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-12) and other references of [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_architecture "Persian architecture"), [Mughal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_architecture "Mughal architecture"), and [Indo-Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Islamic_architecture "Indo-Islamic architecture"). The dome layout and floorplan of the mosque was inspired by the Badshahi Mosque. Its archways are quintessentially [Moorish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture"), and its minarets classically Arab.

In a joint-venture between Italian contractors [Impregilo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impregilo "Impregilo") and [Rizzani de Eccher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizzani_de_Eccher "Rizzani de Eccher"), more than 3,000 workers and 38 sub-contracting companies were conscripted in its construction. The mosque was completed under a second contract by a Joint Venture between ACC and Six Construct (part of Belgian company [BESIX Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BESIX "BESIX")) between 2004 and 2007.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-15) Natural materials were chosen for much of its design and construction due to their long-lasting qualities, including [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble") stone, [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold"), [semi-precious stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemstone "Gemstone"), [crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal "Crystal") and [ceramics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceramic "Ceramic"). Artisans and materials came from many countries including [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria"), especially from [Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus "Damascus") and [Aleppo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleppo "Aleppo"), and some other countries such as [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia "North Macedonia") and the U.A.E.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The intricate flower mosaics decorating the courtyard was designed by the British artist Kevin Dean, who embraced Sheikh Zayed's passionate vision to create a mosque that unites the world, as he chose flowers from the Middle East, such as Tulips, Lilys, and Irises. As inlays of colored marble form exuberant floral patterns that curl and twist gracefully from the edges towards the center adorn the courtyard. While the rest of the Sahan was inlaid with thousands of small pieces of white marble.

## Dimensions and statistics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Dimensions and statistics")]

The mosque is large enough to accommodate over 40,100 worshippers, while the main prayer hall can hold over 7,000. There are two smaller prayer halls, with a capacity of 1,500 each, one of which is the women's prayer hall.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1)

There are four minarets on the four corners of the courtyard which rise about 107 m (351 ft) in height. The [courtyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtyard "Courtyard"), with its floral design, measures about 17,000 m 2 (180,000 sq ft), and is considered to be the largest example of marble mosaic in the world.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1) The exterior and interior are adorned with white marble, giving the mosque a serene and majestic appearance. The marble is inlaid with precious stones like [lapis lazuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapis_lazuli "Lapis lazuli"), [carnelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnelian "Carnelian"), [amethyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amethyst "Amethyst"), [abalone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abalone "Abalone") shell, and [mother of pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_of_pearl "Mother of pearl").

Marble used in the construction included:

*   [Sivec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sivec "Sivec") from [Prilep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prilep "Prilep"), [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia "North Macedonia") was used on the external cladding (115,119 m 2 (1,239,130 sq ft) of cladding has been used on the mosque, including the minarets)
*   [Lasa](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marmo%20di%20Lasa "it:Marmo di Lasa") from [Laas, South Tyrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laas,_South_Tyrol "Laas, South Tyrol"), Italy was used in the internal elevations
*   [Makrana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makrana_marble "Makrana marble") from [Makrana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makrana "Makrana"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") was used in the annexes and offices
*   Acquabianca and Bianco P from [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")
*   East White and Ming Green from [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1)

To compare, the [King Faisal Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Mosque,_Sharjah "King Faisal Mosque, Sharjah") of [Sharjah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharjah "Sharjah"), formerly the largest mosque in [Sharjah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Sharjah "Emirate of Sharjah")[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-KhaleejTimes_07-2015-16) and country, measures 10,000–12,000 m 2 (110,000–130,000 sq ft).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-GulfNews_11-2017-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-TheNational_07-2011-18)

## Architectural features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Architectural features")]

The [carpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpet "Carpet") in the hall is considered by many [_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] to be the world's largest carpet made by Iran's Carpet Company and designed by [Iranian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_peoples "Iranian peoples") artist Ali Khaliqi.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-19) It measures 5,627 m 2 (60,570 sq ft), and was made by around 1,200-1,300 carpet knotters. The weight of this carpet is 35 ton and is predominantly made from [wool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wool "Wool") (originating from [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand") and Iran). There are 2,268,000,000 knots within the carpet and it took approximately two years to complete.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1) The Grand Mosque has seven imported [chandeliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandelier "Chandelier") from the company Faustig in [Munich, Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich,_Germany "Munich, Germany") that incorporate millions of [Swarovski crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swarovski "Swarovski"). The largest chandelier is the second largest known chandelier inside a mosque, the third largest in the world,[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] and has a 10 m (33 ft) diameter and a 15 m (49 ft) height.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1)

The pools along the arcades reflect the mosque's columns, which become illuminated at night. The unique lighting system was designed by lighting architects [Speirs and Major Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speirs_and_Major_Associates "Speirs and Major Associates") to reflect the phases of the moon. Beautiful bluish gray clouds are projected in lights onto the external walls and get brighter and darker according to the phase of the moon.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-20)

The 96 columns in the main prayer hall are clad with marble and inlaid with [mother of pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacre "Nacre"), one of the few places where one can see this craftsmanship.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The [99 names (qualities or attributes) of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_God_in_Islam "Names of God in Islam") ([Allah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_in_Islam "God in Islam")) are featured on the [Qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla") wall in traditional [Kufic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kufic "Kufic") calligraphy, designed by the prominent UAE calligrapher — Mohammed Mandi Al Tamimi. The Qibla wall also features subtle fibre-optic lighting, which is integrated as part of the organic design.

In total, three calligraphy styles — [Naskhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naskh_(script) "Naskh (script)"), _[Thuluth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuluth "Thuluth")_ and [Kufic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kufic "Kufic") — are used throughout the mosque and were drafted by Mohammed Mandi Al Tamimi of the UAE, Farouk Haddad of [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria") and Mohammed Allam of [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1)

The **Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): جَامِع ٱلشَّيْخ زَايِد ٱلْكَبِيْر _Jāmiʿ Aš-Šaykh Zāyid Al-Kabīr_) is a mosque located in [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"), the capital city of the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1) It is the [country's largest mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mosques_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "List of mosques in the United Arab Emirates"), and is the key place of worship for [daily Islamic prayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salah "Salah"). There is a [smaller replica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque,_Solo "Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, Solo") of this mosque in [Surakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surakarta "Surakarta"), a city in [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-TheNational_11-2022-2)

The Grand Mosque was constructed between 1994 and 2007 and was inaugurated in December 2007.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-3) The building complex measures approximately 290 by 420 m (950 by 1,380 ft), covering an area of more than 12 hectares (30 acres), excluding exterior landscaping and vehicle parking. The main axis of the building is rotated about 12° south of true west, aligning it in the direction of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca, [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").

The project was launched by the late president of the U.A.E., [Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh "Sheikh")[Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_bin_Sultan_Al_Nahyan "Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan"), who wanted to establish a structure that would unite the cultural diversity of the Islamic world with the historical and modern values of architecture and art.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-4) In 2004, Sheikh Zayed died and was buried in the courtyard of the mosque.

Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque Center (SZGMC) offices are located in the west [minarets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret"). SZGMC manages the day-to-day operations and serves as a center of learning and discovery through its educational cultural activities and visitor programs. The library, located in the northeast minaret, serves the community with classic books and publications addressing a range of Islamic subjects: [sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_in_the_medieval_Islamic_world "Science in the medieval Islamic world"), [civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Golden_Age "Islamic Golden Age"), [calligraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calligraphy "Islamic calligraphy"), the [arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_art "Islamic art"), and coins, including some rare publications. The collection comprises material in a broad range of languages, including Arabic, English, French, Italian, Spanish, German, and Korean. For two years running, it was voted the world's second favourite landmark by [TripAdvisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TripAdvisor "TripAdvisor").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-5)

The Grand Mosque has been a significant destination for visiting foreign leaders during official state visits to the [UAE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"). Notable visitors include [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-6) the then US Vice President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-7) Australian Prime Minister [Anthony Albanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Albanese "Anthony Albanese").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-8) and Indian Prime Minister [Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-9)

## Design and construction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Design and construction")]

The mosque was built under the guidance and supervision of Sheikh Zayed, who was buried here after his death in 2004. It features 82 domes, more than 1,000 columns, 24-carat-gold gilded chandeliers and the world's largest hand-knotted carpet. The main prayer hall is dominated by one of the largest chandeliers. The mosque was designed under the management of the [Syrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrians "Syrians") architect Youssef Abdelke, and three other architectural designers from [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria") who completed the design and worked on developing it, Basem Barghouti, Moataz Al-Halabi, and Imad Malas.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-10)

The mosque's architect Yusef Abdelki took inspiration from a number of sources: the [Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_al-Abbas_al-Mursi_Mosque "Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi Mosque") in [Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria "Alexandria"), designed by [Mario Rossi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Rossi_(architect) "Mario Rossi (architect)") in the 1920s;[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-11) the [Badshahi Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badshahi_Mosque "Badshahi Mosque") in [Lahore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore "Lahore"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan");[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-12) and other references of [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_architecture "Persian architecture"), [Mughal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_architecture "Mughal architecture"), and [Indo-Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Islamic_architecture "Indo-Islamic architecture"). The dome layout and floorplan of the mosque was inspired by the Badshahi Mosque. Its archways are quintessentially [Moorish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture"), and its minarets classically Arab.

In a joint-venture between Italian contractors [Impregilo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impregilo "Impregilo") and [Rizzani de Eccher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizzani_de_Eccher "Rizzani de Eccher"), more than 3,000 workers and 38 sub-contracting companies were conscripted in its construction. The mosque was completed under a second contract by a Joint Venture between ACC and Six Construct (part of Belgian company [BESIX Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BESIX "BESIX")) between 2004 and 2007.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-15) Natural materials were chosen for much of its design and construction due to their long-lasting qualities, including [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble") stone, [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold"), [semi-precious stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemstone "Gemstone"), [crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal "Crystal") and [ceramics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceramic "Ceramic"). Artisans and materials came from many countries including [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria"), especially from [Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus "Damascus") and [Aleppo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleppo "Aleppo"), and some other countries such as [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia "North Macedonia") and the U.A.E.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The intricate flower mosaics decorating the courtyard was designed by the British artist Kevin Dean, who embraced Sheikh Zayed's passionate vision to create a mosque that unites the world, as he chose flowers from the Middle East, such as Tulips, Lilys, and Irises. As inlays of colored marble form exuberant floral patterns that curl and twist gracefully from the edges towards the center adorn the courtyard. While the rest of the Sahan was inlaid with thousands of small pieces of white marble.

## Dimensions and statistics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Dimensions and statistics")]

The mosque is large enough to accommodate over 40,100 worshippers, while the main prayer hall can hold over 7,000. There are two smaller prayer halls, with a capacity of 1,500 each, one of which is the women's prayer hall.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1)

There are four minarets on the four corners of the courtyard which rise about 107 m (351 ft) in height. The [courtyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtyard "Courtyard"), with its floral design, measures about 17,000 m 2 (180,000 sq ft), and is considered to be the largest example of marble mosaic in the world.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1) The exterior and interior are adorned with white marble, giving the mosque a serene and majestic appearance. The marble is inlaid with precious stones like [lapis lazuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapis_lazuli "Lapis lazuli"), [carnelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnelian "Carnelian"), [amethyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amethyst "Amethyst"), [abalone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abalone "Abalone") shell, and [mother of pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_of_pearl "Mother of pearl").

Marble used in the construction included:

*   [Sivec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sivec "Sivec") from [Prilep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prilep "Prilep"), [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia "North Macedonia") was used on the external cladding (115,119 m 2 (1,239,130 sq ft) of cladding has been used on the mosque, including the minarets)
*   [Lasa](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marmo%20di%20Lasa "it:Marmo di Lasa") from [Laas, South Tyrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laas,_South_Tyrol "Laas, South Tyrol"), Italy was used in the internal elevations
*   [Makrana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makrana_marble "Makrana marble") from [Makrana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makrana "Makrana"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") was used in the annexes and offices
*   Acquabianca and Bianco P from [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")
*   East White and Ming Green from [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1)

To compare, the [King Faisal Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Faisal_Mosque,_Sharjah "King Faisal Mosque, Sharjah") of [Sharjah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharjah "Sharjah"), formerly the largest mosque in [Sharjah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Sharjah "Emirate of Sharjah")[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-KhaleejTimes_07-2015-16) and country, measures 10,000–12,000 m 2 (110,000–130,000 sq ft).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-GulfNews_11-2017-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-TheNational_07-2011-18)

## Architectural features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Architectural features")]

The [carpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpet "Carpet") in the hall is considered by many [_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] to be the world's largest carpet made by Iran's Carpet Company and designed by [Iranian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_peoples "Iranian peoples") artist Ali Khaliqi.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-19) It measures 5,627 m 2 (60,570 sq ft), and was made by around 1,200-1,300 carpet knotters. The weight of this carpet is 35 ton and is predominantly made from [wool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wool "Wool") (originating from [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand") and Iran). There are 2,268,000,000 knots within the carpet and it took approximately two years to complete.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1) The Grand Mosque has seven imported [chandeliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandelier "Chandelier") from the company Faustig in [Munich, Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich,_Germany "Munich, Germany") that incorporate millions of [Swarovski crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swarovski "Swarovski"). The largest chandelier is the second largest known chandelier inside a mosque, the third largest in the world,[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] and has a 10 m (33 ft) diameter and a 15 m (49 ft) height.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1)

The pools along the arcades reflect the mosque's columns, which become illuminated at night. The unique lighting system was designed by lighting architects [Speirs and Major Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speirs_and_Major_Associates "Speirs and Major Associates") to reflect the phases of the moon. Beautiful bluish gray clouds are projected in lights onto the external walls and get brighter and darker according to the phase of the moon.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-20)

The 96 columns in the main prayer hall are clad with marble and inlaid with [mother of pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacre "Nacre"), one of the few places where one can see this craftsmanship.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The [99 names (qualities or attributes) of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_God_in_Islam "Names of God in Islam") ([Allah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_in_Islam "God in Islam")) are featured on the [Qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla") wall in traditional [Kufic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kufic "Kufic") calligraphy, designed by the prominent UAE calligrapher — Mohammed Mandi Al Tamimi. The Qibla wall also features subtle fibre-optic lighting, which is integrated as part of the organic design.

In total, three calligraphy styles — [Naskhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naskh_(script) "Naskh (script)"), _[Thuluth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuluth "Thuluth")_ and [Kufic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kufic "Kufic") — are used throughout the mosque and were drafted by Mohammed Mandi Al Tamimi of the UAE, Farouk Haddad of [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria") and Mohammed Allam of [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Zayed_Grand_Mosque#cite_note-SZGMC-1)

The **Bay'ah Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مسجد البيعة), also known as the **Mosque of 'Aqaba Hill** and the **Aqabah Mosque**, is a [Sunni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunni_Islam "Sunni Islam") Muslim [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque"), located outside Mecca in [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay'ah_Mosque#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay'ah_Mosque#cite_note-2) below the Wadi [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina,_Saudi_Arabia "Mina, Saudi Arabia").

It was built at the request of Caliph [Abu Ja'far al-Mansur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Ja'far_al-Mansur "Abu Ja'far al-Mansur") in 761 [CE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era") at the site of al-Bay'ah, i.e. the place where the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_of_Islam "Prophets of Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") met with the [Ansar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ansar_(Islam) "Ansar (Islam)") (the supporters), and they took the pledge ('bay'ah', hence the name) of 'Aqaba.

The mosque has an open courtyard.

The **Bay'ah Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مسجد البيعة), also known as the **Mosque of 'Aqaba Hill** and the **Aqabah Mosque**, is a [Sunni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunni_Islam "Sunni Islam") Muslim [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque"), located outside Mecca in [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay'ah_Mosque#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay'ah_Mosque#cite_note-2) below the Wadi [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina,_Saudi_Arabia "Mina, Saudi Arabia").

It was built at the request of Caliph [Abu Ja'far al-Mansur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Ja'far_al-Mansur "Abu Ja'far al-Mansur") in 761 [CE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era") at the site of al-Bay'ah, i.e. the place where the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_of_Islam "Prophets of Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") met with the [Ansar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ansar_(Islam) "Ansar (Islam)") (the supporters), and they took the pledge ('bay'ah', hence the name) of 'Aqaba.

The mosque has an open courtyard.

**Al-Ji'rana** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): ٱلْجِعْرَانَة, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Al-Jiʿrānah_) is a village in [Mecca Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_Province "Mecca Province"), in [western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz")[Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-1) A [boundary of the Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miqat#Al-%E1%B8%A4aram "Miqat"), it is located 18 miles (29 kilometres) northeast of Mecca.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-HajjUmrahPlanner-2)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Ji%27rana&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

See also: [Geography of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Saudi_Arabia "Geography of Saudi Arabia"), [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), and [History of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia "History of Saudi Arabia")

It was here in the [7th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_century "7th century") that the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_and_messengers_in_Islam "Prophets and messengers in Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") distributed spoils of war among [his allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Companions_of_the_Prophet "Companions of the Prophet"), after the battles of [Hunain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hunayn "Battle of Hunayn") and [Autas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Autas "Battle of Autas"), and before the [siege of Ta'if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Ta'if "Siege of Ta'if").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-4)

Al-Ji'rana was mentioned by the [8th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_century "8th century")[Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs") historian [Al-Waqidi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Waqidi "Al-Waqidi"). In his _Kitab al-Tarikh wa al-Maghazi_ ("Book of History and Campaigns"), Al-Waqidi describes two ancient sanctuaries in al-Ji'rana visited by [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam") on his journey on [dhu al-qa'da](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Qadah "Dhu al-Qadah") of the eighth year after the [Hijrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah "Hijrah"): _\_al-masjid al-aqṣā\__ ("the farthest mosque") and _\_al-masjid al-adnā\_ (_"the closest mosque"_)._[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:0-6) This was also mentioned by [Al-Azraqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Azraqi "Al-Azraqi"), a [9th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_century "9th century")[Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") commentator and historian.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:0-6)

According to the [Qur'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran"), Muhammad was transported to a site named _al-masjid al-ʾaqṣā_ ("the furthest place of prayer") during his [Night Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra_and_Mi'raj "Isra and Mi'raj").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-17th2-7) The Qur'an does not mention the exact location of "the furthest place of prayer".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Khatib-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:9-9) The actual meaning of the phrase is debated in both early Islamic and contemporary sources. According to the [Encyclopaedia of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclopaedia_of_Islam "Encyclopaedia of Islam"), the term was originally understood as a reference to a site in the heavens.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:8-10) Another group of Islamic scholars understood the story of Muhammad's ascension from Al-Aqsa Mosque as relating to Jerusalem.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:8-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Colby2008-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:10-12) Eventually, a consensus emerged around the identification of the "furthest place of prayer" with [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem"), and by implication the [Temple Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_Mount "Temple Mount").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Colby20082-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-14)

In 1953, British Islamic scholar [Alfred Guillaume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Guillaume "Alfred Guillaume") suggested that Al-Ju'ranah was the location of [Al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa "Al-Aqsa") described in the Qur'an as the destination of Muhammad's Night Journey.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-15) He based his theory on the writings of Al-Waqidi and Al-Azraqi. In 1959, French art historian [Oleg Grabar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Grabar "Oleg Grabar") wrote this theory was convincing.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:102-16) This theory has received backing from [Youssef Ziedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youssef_Ziedan "Youssef Ziedan"), [Mordechai Kedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordechai_Kedar "Mordechai Kedar"), [Yitzhak Reiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Reiter "Yitzhak Reiter"), and Suleiman al-Tarawneh in recent years.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:2-18) These historians also support the view according which the [Umayyad dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_dynasty "Umayyad dynasty")'s political objectives contributed to the sanctification of Jerusalem in Islam, as they sought to compete with the religious importance of Mecca, which was then ruled by their rival, [Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:82-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-20)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:2-18) The theory has been criticized as a "claim [which] merely consists of subjective interpretations".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-21)

In November 2020, Saudi lawyer Osama Yamani promoted this theory in an opinion article in the Saudi newspaper [Okaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okaz "Okaz").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-23) The article sparked outrage from [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") around the world, with some writers claiming it was fabricated to justify the [decision of some Gulf countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Accords "Abraham Accords") to [normalize ties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab-Israeli_normalization "Arab-Israeli normalization") with [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-24)

If Muslims interpret the qur'anic phrase "the sacred place of prayer" in diverse ways, one encounters even more debate over the destination of the night journey, the "furthest place of prayer". Guillaume's careful analysis of the earliest texts (al-Waqidi and al-Azraqi, both in the later second century A.H.) has convincingly shown that the Koranic reference to the masjid al-aqsa applies specifically to al-Ji'ranah, near Mekkah, where there were two sanctuaries (masjid al-adnai and masjid al-aqsa), and where Muhammad so-journed in dha al-qa'dah of the eighth year after the Hijrah.

**Al-Ji'rana** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): ٱلْجِعْرَانَة, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Al-Jiʿrānah_) is a village in [Mecca Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_Province "Mecca Province"), in [western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz")[Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-1) A [boundary of the Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miqat#Al-%E1%B8%A4aram "Miqat"), it is located 18 miles (29 kilometres) northeast of Mecca.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-HajjUmrahPlanner-2)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Ji%27rana&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

See also: [Geography of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Saudi_Arabia "Geography of Saudi Arabia"), [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), and [History of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia "History of Saudi Arabia")

It was here in the [7th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_century "7th century") that the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_and_messengers_in_Islam "Prophets and messengers in Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") distributed spoils of war among [his allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Companions_of_the_Prophet "Companions of the Prophet"), after the battles of [Hunain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hunayn "Battle of Hunayn") and [Autas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Autas "Battle of Autas"), and before the [siege of Ta'if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Ta'if "Siege of Ta'if").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-4)

Al-Ji'rana was mentioned by the [8th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_century "8th century")[Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs") historian [Al-Waqidi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Waqidi "Al-Waqidi"). In his _Kitab al-Tarikh wa al-Maghazi_ ("Book of History and Campaigns"), Al-Waqidi describes two ancient sanctuaries in al-Ji'rana visited by [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam") on his journey on [dhu al-qa'da](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Qadah "Dhu al-Qadah") of the eighth year after the [Hijrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah "Hijrah"): _\_al-masjid al-aqṣā\__ ("the farthest mosque") and _\_al-masjid al-adnā\_ (_"the closest mosque"_)._[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:0-6) This was also mentioned by [Al-Azraqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Azraqi "Al-Azraqi"), a [9th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_century "9th century")[Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") commentator and historian.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:0-6)

According to the [Qur'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran"), Muhammad was transported to a site named _al-masjid al-ʾaqṣā_ ("the furthest place of prayer") during his [Night Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra_and_Mi'raj "Isra and Mi'raj").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-17th2-7) The Qur'an does not mention the exact location of "the furthest place of prayer".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Khatib-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:9-9) The actual meaning of the phrase is debated in both early Islamic and contemporary sources. According to the [Encyclopaedia of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclopaedia_of_Islam "Encyclopaedia of Islam"), the term was originally understood as a reference to a site in the heavens.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:8-10) Another group of Islamic scholars understood the story of Muhammad's ascension from Al-Aqsa Mosque as relating to Jerusalem.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:8-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Colby2008-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:10-12) Eventually, a consensus emerged around the identification of the "furthest place of prayer" with [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem"), and by implication the [Temple Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_Mount "Temple Mount").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Colby20082-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-14)

In 1953, British Islamic scholar [Alfred Guillaume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Guillaume "Alfred Guillaume") suggested that Al-Ju'ranah was the location of [Al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa "Al-Aqsa") described in the Qur'an as the destination of Muhammad's Night Journey.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-15) He based his theory on the writings of Al-Waqidi and Al-Azraqi. In 1959, French art historian [Oleg Grabar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Grabar "Oleg Grabar") wrote this theory was convincing.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:102-16) This theory has received backing from [Youssef Ziedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youssef_Ziedan "Youssef Ziedan"), [Mordechai Kedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordechai_Kedar "Mordechai Kedar"), [Yitzhak Reiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Reiter "Yitzhak Reiter"), and Suleiman al-Tarawneh in recent years.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:2-18) These historians also support the view according which the [Umayyad dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_dynasty "Umayyad dynasty")'s political objectives contributed to the sanctification of Jerusalem in Islam, as they sought to compete with the religious importance of Mecca, which was then ruled by their rival, [Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:82-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-20)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:2-18) The theory has been criticized as a "claim [which] merely consists of subjective interpretations".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-21)

In November 2020, Saudi lawyer Osama Yamani promoted this theory in an opinion article in the Saudi newspaper [Okaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okaz "Okaz").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-23) The article sparked outrage from [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") around the world, with some writers claiming it was fabricated to justify the [decision of some Gulf countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Accords "Abraham Accords") to [normalize ties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab-Israeli_normalization "Arab-Israeli normalization") with [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-24)

**Al-Ji'rana** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): ٱلْجِعْرَانَة, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Al-Jiʿrānah_) is a village in [Mecca Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_Province "Mecca Province"), in [western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz")[Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-1) A [boundary of the Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miqat#Al-%E1%B8%A4aram "Miqat"), it is located 18 miles (29 kilometres) northeast of Mecca.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-HajjUmrahPlanner-2)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Ji%27rana&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

See also: [Geography of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Saudi_Arabia "Geography of Saudi Arabia"), [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), and [History of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia "History of Saudi Arabia")

It was here in the [7th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_century "7th century") that the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_and_messengers_in_Islam "Prophets and messengers in Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") distributed spoils of war among [his allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Companions_of_the_Prophet "Companions of the Prophet"), after the battles of [Hunain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hunayn "Battle of Hunayn") and [Autas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Autas "Battle of Autas"), and before the [siege of Ta'if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Ta'if "Siege of Ta'if").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-4)

Al-Ji'rana was mentioned by the [8th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_century "8th century")[Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs") historian [Al-Waqidi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Waqidi "Al-Waqidi"). In his _Kitab al-Tarikh wa al-Maghazi_ ("Book of History and Campaigns"), Al-Waqidi describes two ancient sanctuaries in al-Ji'rana visited by [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam") on his journey on [dhu al-qa'da](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Qadah "Dhu al-Qadah") of the eighth year after the [Hijrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah "Hijrah"): _\_al-masjid al-aqṣā\__ ("the farthest mosque") and _\_al-masjid al-adnā\_ (_"the closest mosque"_)._[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:0-6) This was also mentioned by [Al-Azraqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Azraqi "Al-Azraqi"), a [9th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_century "9th century")[Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") commentator and historian.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:0-6)

According to the [Qur'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran"), Muhammad was transported to a site named _al-masjid al-ʾaqṣā_ ("the furthest place of prayer") during his [Night Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra_and_Mi'raj "Isra and Mi'raj").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-17th2-7) The Qur'an does not mention the exact location of "the furthest place of prayer".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Khatib-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:9-9) The actual meaning of the phrase is debated in both early Islamic and contemporary sources. According to the [Encyclopaedia of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclopaedia_of_Islam "Encyclopaedia of Islam"), the term was originally understood as a reference to a site in the heavens.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:8-10) Another group of Islamic scholars understood the story of Muhammad's ascension from Al-Aqsa Mosque as relating to Jerusalem.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:8-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Colby2008-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:10-12) Eventually, a consensus emerged around the identification of the "furthest place of prayer" with [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem"), and by implication the [Temple Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_Mount "Temple Mount").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Colby20082-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-14)

In 1953, British Islamic scholar [Alfred Guillaume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Guillaume "Alfred Guillaume") suggested that Al-Ju'ranah was the location of [Al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa "Al-Aqsa") described in the Qur'an as the destination of Muhammad's Night Journey.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-15) He based his theory on the writings of Al-Waqidi and Al-Azraqi. In 1959, French art historian [Oleg Grabar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Grabar "Oleg Grabar") wrote this theory was convincing.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:102-16) This theory has received backing from [Youssef Ziedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youssef_Ziedan "Youssef Ziedan"), [Mordechai Kedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordechai_Kedar "Mordechai Kedar"), [Yitzhak Reiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Reiter "Yitzhak Reiter"), and Suleiman al-Tarawneh in recent years.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:2-18) These historians also support the view according which the [Umayyad dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_dynasty "Umayyad dynasty")'s political objectives contributed to the sanctification of Jerusalem in Islam, as they sought to compete with the religious importance of Mecca, which was then ruled by their rival, [Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:82-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-20)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:2-18) The theory has been criticized as a "claim [which] merely consists of subjective interpretations".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-21)

In November 2020, Saudi lawyer Osama Yamani promoted this theory in an opinion article in the Saudi newspaper [Okaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okaz "Okaz").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-23) The article sparked outrage from [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") around the world, with some writers claiming it was fabricated to justify the [decision of some Gulf countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Accords "Abraham Accords") to [normalize ties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab-Israeli_normalization "Arab-Israeli normalization") with [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-24)

For this verse, tradition gives three interpretations: The oldest one, which disappears from the more recent commentaries, detects an allusion to Muhammad's Ascension to Heaven. This explanation interprets the expression al-masjid al-aksa, "the further place of worship" in the sense of "Heaven" and, in fact, in the older tradition isra is often used as synonymous with miradj (see Isl., vi, 14). The second explanation, the only one given in all the more modern commentaries, interprets masjid al-aksa as "Jerusalem" and this for no very apparent reason. It seems to have been an Umayyad device intended to further the glorification of Jerusalem as against that of the holy territory (cf. Goldziher, Muh. Stud., ii, 55-6; Isl, vi, 13 ff), then ruled by Abd Allah b. al-Zubayr. Al-Tabarl seems to reject it. He does not mention it in his History and seems rather to adopt the first explanation.

If Muslims interpret the qur'anic phrase "the sacred place of prayer" in diverse ways, one encounters even more debate over the destination of the night journey, the "furthest place of prayer". From the earliest extant Muslim texts, it becomes clear that a group of Muslims from the beginning interpreted "furthest place of prayer" with the city of Jerusalem in general and its Herodian/Solomonic Temple in particular. It is equally clear that other early Muslims disputed this connection, identifying the "furthest place of prayer" instead as a reference to a site in the heavens. Eventually a general consensus formed around the idea that Muhammad's journey did indeed take him to Jerusalem. Even if the night journey verse were thought to refer first and foremost to the terrestrial portion of Muhammad's journey, nevertheless for centuries scholars and storytellers also continued to connect this verse with the idea of an ascent through the levels of the heavens.

**Al-Ji'rana** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): ٱلْجِعْرَانَة, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_Al-Jiʿrānah_) is a village in [Mecca Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_Province "Mecca Province"), in [western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz")[Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-1) A [boundary of the Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miqat#Al-%E1%B8%A4aram "Miqat"), it is located 18 miles (29 kilometres) northeast of Mecca.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-HajjUmrahPlanner-2)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al-Ji%27rana&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

See also: [Geography of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Saudi_Arabia "Geography of Saudi Arabia"), [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), and [History of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia "History of Saudi Arabia")

It was here in the [7th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_century "7th century") that the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_and_messengers_in_Islam "Prophets and messengers in Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") distributed spoils of war among [his allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Companions_of_the_Prophet "Companions of the Prophet"), after the battles of [Hunain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hunayn "Battle of Hunayn") and [Autas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Autas "Battle of Autas"), and before the [siege of Ta'if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Ta'if "Siege of Ta'if").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-4)

Al-Ji'rana was mentioned by the [8th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_century "8th century")[Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs") historian [Al-Waqidi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Waqidi "Al-Waqidi"). In his _Kitab al-Tarikh wa al-Maghazi_ ("Book of History and Campaigns"), Al-Waqidi describes two ancient sanctuaries in al-Ji'rana visited by [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam") on his journey on [dhu al-qa'da](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Qadah "Dhu al-Qadah") of the eighth year after the [Hijrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah "Hijrah"): _\_al-masjid al-aqṣā\__ ("the farthest mosque") and _\_al-masjid al-adnā\_ (_"the closest mosque"_)._[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:0-6) This was also mentioned by [Al-Azraqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Azraqi "Al-Azraqi"), a [9th-century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_century "9th century")[Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") commentator and historian.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:0-6)

According to the [Qur'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran"), Muhammad was transported to a site named _al-masjid al-ʾaqṣā_ ("the furthest place of prayer") during his [Night Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra_and_Mi'raj "Isra and Mi'raj").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-17th2-7) The Qur'an does not mention the exact location of "the furthest place of prayer".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Khatib-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:9-9) The actual meaning of the phrase is debated in both early Islamic and contemporary sources. According to the [Encyclopaedia of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclopaedia_of_Islam "Encyclopaedia of Islam"), the term was originally understood as a reference to a site in the heavens.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:8-10) Another group of Islamic scholars understood the story of Muhammad's ascension from Al-Aqsa Mosque as relating to Jerusalem.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:8-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Colby2008-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:10-12) Eventually, a consensus emerged around the identification of the "furthest place of prayer" with [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem"), and by implication the [Temple Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_Mount "Temple Mount").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-Colby20082-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-14)

In 1953, British Islamic scholar [Alfred Guillaume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Guillaume "Alfred Guillaume") suggested that Al-Ju'ranah was the location of [Al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa "Al-Aqsa") described in the Qur'an as the destination of Muhammad's Night Journey.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-15) He based his theory on the writings of Al-Waqidi and Al-Azraqi. In 1959, French art historian [Oleg Grabar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Grabar "Oleg Grabar") wrote this theory was convincing.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:102-16) This theory has received backing from [Youssef Ziedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youssef_Ziedan "Youssef Ziedan"), [Mordechai Kedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordechai_Kedar "Mordechai Kedar"), [Yitzhak Reiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Reiter "Yitzhak Reiter"), and Suleiman al-Tarawneh in recent years.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:2-18) These historians also support the view according which the [Umayyad dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_dynasty "Umayyad dynasty")'s political objectives contributed to the sanctification of Jerusalem in Islam, as they sought to compete with the religious importance of Mecca, which was then ruled by their rival, [Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:82-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-20)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-:2-18) The theory has been criticized as a "claim [which] merely consists of subjective interpretations".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-21)

In November 2020, Saudi lawyer Osama Yamani promoted this theory in an opinion article in the Saudi newspaper [Okaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okaz "Okaz").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-23) The article sparked outrage from [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") around the world, with some writers claiming it was fabricated to justify the [decision of some Gulf countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Accords "Abraham Accords") to [normalize ties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab-Israeli_normalization "Arab-Israeli normalization") with [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_Al-Ji'ranah#cite_note-24)
